At the verifier boundary, use exhaustive switches over the state. Force downstream callers to handle each branch. If your language supports pattern matching, lean on it to eliminate default fall-through behaviors.

Treat absence as an opportunity to request or fall back

If a required field is missing, decide whether to:

Prompt the holder to supply it (if applicable).

Proceed with reduced assurance and log the state.

Deny the request explicitly as “unverifiable,” not “invalid.” The right action depends on your policy and context; the key is keeping “unverifiable” distinct.

Make “invalid” a narrow, technical category

Invalid should mean “structured wrong,” “bad signature,” or “contradiction.” It shouldn’t include “not provided,” “not bound,” or “not present yet.” Narrow “invalid” ensures you don’t over-penalize users for the system’s constraints.

Propagate state through APIs and UX

Expose the state in API responses: include status: "unverifiable" with a short note. Avoid returning false or 0 as a sentinel for “missing.” In UX, explain that more evidence is needed or that a different path is available.

Beware implicit type coercions

JSON, databases, and ORMs often coerce nulls to zero or false. Audit these boundaries. Ensure your serializers and persistence layers preserve state labels rather than defaulting values.

Test for fairness: counterfactuals

Put fairness into tests. For example: if “proofOfX” is missing, does the system deny or ask for more evidence? Are there alternative flows? Keep tests that assert the difference between “unverifiable” and “invalid.”

Explicit verification outcomes

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Status = Literal["accepted", "unverifiable", "invalid"]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class FieldCheck:
    name: str
    status: Status
    note: str | None = None

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

More state complexity vs simplicity: Explicit states add a little code. The clarity and fairness gains are worth it.

UX friction vs silent denial: Asking for more evidence can add steps. Silent denials are worse. Balance friction with guidance.

Logging granularity vs privacy: Notes improve debugging; ensure they contain no sensitive data.

Failure modes

“Hidden coercion”: Tooling collapses null to false. Solution: audit boundaries and enforce state labels.

“Catch-all invalid”: Development shortcuts treat everything negative as invalid. Solution: write exhaustive switches and linters.

“Unverifiable loop”: Repeated prompts for evidence without alternative paths. Solution: define fallback policies clearly.

Try it yourself

Replace boolean checks for critical credential fields with stateful outcomes (“accepted,” “unverifiable,” “invalid”).

Expose the state in your verifier’s API. Track how often “unverifiable” occurs and address UX with prompts or fallbacks.

Add tests that assert denials only occur for “invalid,” not “unverifiable.”

Further reading

  • W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
  • Java pattern matching for switch

atom:entry.atom:title: Docker in CI: The Real Cost of Docker-in-Docker
atom:entry.atom:summary: Understand Docker-in-Docker trade-offs, protect daemon access, and make container-dependent CI tests fail closed.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Docker-in-Docker (DinD) can make CI feel simple: start a job, build an image, run container-based tests. The convenience comes with a real isolation decision. Privileged DinD can weaken the boundary around the runner; mounting the host Docker socket can give a build step powerful control over the host daemon.

Teams still choose these patterns because they support familiar workflows. The important thing is to make the choice explicit, restrict which code can use it, and avoid a “green” result when container tests never ran.

First, know which daemon the job is using

“Docker in CI” does not always mean DinD. Some runners expose a Docker daemon to the job; DinD starts a separate Docker daemon inside a service container. A mounted /var/run/docker.sock is a third pattern: the job’s Docker CLI talks to the host daemon. These setups have different isolation properties. Document the runner architecture before relying on it.

Verify the daemon before running tests

Make readiness an explicit step. If the daemon is missing or unresponsive, stop the job before it reports container-dependent tests as successful:

# Run only on a runner configured to provide Docker access.
set -eu
docker version
docker info

IMAGE="aceu-trust-demo:${GITHUB_SHA:-local}"
docker build --tag "$IMAGE" .
docker run --rm "$IMAGE" pytest -q

For an actual DinD service, the job also needs to wait for that service’s daemon to become available. A fixed sleep is brittle; use a bounded readiness loop and fail with a clear message if the daemon never responds.

Do not silently skip container-dependent tests

If the daemon is a prerequisite, the test should fail when Docker is unavailable. Avoid code that catches every exception and quietly returns a passing or skipped result in a required CI job:

import subprocess


def docker_available() -> bool:
    try:
        subprocess.run(
            ["docker", "info"],
            check=True,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=10,
        )
        return True
    except (FileNotFoundError, subprocess.CalledProcessError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
        return False


def test_containerized_health_check_requires_docker():
    assert docker_available(), "Docker daemon is required for this test"
    # Continue with the containerized test flow.

Tag Docker-dependent tests so developers can distinguish them from pure unit tests, but keep them required in the CI path that claims to validate the container.

Choose the access pattern with eyes open

  • Privileged DinD: familiar and flexible, but grants elevated capabilities to the service container. Restrict it to trusted workflows and isolate the runner.
  • Host socket mount: avoids starting another daemon, but the mounted socket can let job code control the host Docker daemon. Treat access as highly privileged.
  • Daemonless or remote builders: can reduce direct daemon exposure in some environments, but require setup and may change the build workflow.

In every case, pin build images, keep credentials scoped, avoid running untrusted pull-request code on privileged self-hosted runners, and clean up jobs so containers and volumes do not leak into later runs.

Watch for isolation leaks and flaky runners

Look for unexpected host mounts, files written outside the workspace, orphaned containers, and daemon failures. Runner fleets can have transient problems. A documented single retry can filter a brief infrastructure hiccup, but repeated failure should remain visible and investigated—not retried until a broken test turns green.

Trade-offs to discuss with the team

  • Speed vs. isolation: DinD is familiar; stricter alternatives can require more setup.
  • Fail closed vs. ergonomics: blocking on daemon failure catches false greens but can be frustrating when runner health is poor. Give contributors a clear error and retry path.
  • Socket mount vs. privileged mode: neither is a free isolation boundary. Limit trusted code and runner scope for either design.

Try it in your CI

  1. Write down whether jobs use host Docker, a mounted socket, or a separate DinD service.
  2. Add a daemon readiness check before any container-dependent test.
  3. Make those tests fail if Docker is unavailable; do not silently skip them.
  4. Evaluate a daemonless or remote builder against your runner threat model.
  5. Document when one retry is appropriate and when repeated failure needs investigation.

Closing thought

DinD can be pragmatic, but it should never be invisible. Verify the daemon, make tests fail closed, and choose an isolation pattern that matches what the CI job is trusted to do.

Further reading

  • Protect access to the Docker daemon socket
  • Docker Engine security
  • GitHub Actions secure-use guidance

atom:entry.atom:title: Oracle DB: invoker's vs definer's rights for least-privilege code
atom:entry.atom:summary: A simple rule of thumb for choosing AUTHID, with two small procedures that show the difference.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

PL/SQL runs with one of two sets of privileges: the owner's (definer's rights) or the caller's (invoker's rights). Choosing the wrong one is how a harmless helper procedure ends up with far more reach than anyone intended.

I wanted a decision path I can apply in seconds and defend in a code review.

Options and trade-offs

  • Definer's rights (AUTHID DEFINER, the default): privileges come from the owner. Callers need only EXECUTE, and the risk is an owner with broad privileges.
  • Invoker's rights (AUTHID CURRENT_USER): the code works within the caller's own privileges, which suits shared code across schemas or tenants. Callers need access to every object it touches.

My recommendation

Make shared, reusable code invoker's rights, so it can never do more than the person calling it. Use definer's rights for a small number of deliberate entry points that expose one action without handing out table privileges, and restrict who may call them.

Worked example

An invoker's rights procedure resolves unqualified names at run time in the caller's schema, so it reads the caller's own orders table.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE app_util.list_my_orders
  AUTHID CURRENT_USER
AS
BEGIN
  FOR r IN (SELECT order_id, status FROM orders) LOOP
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE(r.order_id || ' ' || r.status);
  END LOOP;
END;
/

A definer's rights entry point is the opposite. It performs one privileged action on the owner's data, and ACCESSIBLE BY restricts which program units may call it.

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE app_admin.close_period (p_period IN NUMBER)
  AUTHID DEFINER
  ACCESSIBLE BY (PACKAGE app_api.billing)
AS
BEGIN
  UPDATE fiscal_periods SET status = 'CLOSED' WHERE period_id = p_period;
END;
/
GRANT EXECUTE ON app_admin.close_period TO billing_role;

A few facts that help in practice. Roles are disabled inside definer's rights code, so the owner needs direct grants. Since Oracle Database 12c, an invoker's rights unit can use the caller's privileges only if its owner has the INHERIT PRIVILEGES privilege on the caller, or INHERIT ANY PRIVILEGES. Anonymous blocks run with the privileges of whoever executes them.

Checklist

  1. Decide who should own the effective privileges before writing the code.
  2. For invoker's rights, confirm callers have the object privileges the code needs.
  3. Keep definer's rights units small, and keep the owner's privileges minimal.
  4. Use ACCESSIBLE BY to limit callers of sensitive procedures.
  5. Document entry points and who calls them, and audit executions.
  6. Review dynamic SQL, because it resolves names at run time.

Where this doesn't apply

Anonymous blocks already behave like invoker's rights, so the choice does not apply to them.

One honest limitation

Invoker's rights with static SQL expects matching objects to exist for the owner at compile time and for the caller at run time. Plan schema design so those differences do not produce subtle errors.

Sources

  • Oracle Database PL/SQL Language Reference: Invoker's Rights and Definer's Rights (AUTHID Property)
  • Oracle Database Security Guide: Managing Security for Definer's Rights and Invoker's Rights
  • Oracle Database PL/SQL Language Reference: ACCESSIBLE BY Clause

atom:entry.atom:title: CPU-Only, By Design: Building an Edge-AI Service Without Assuming Accelerators
atom:entry.atom:summary: Design edge inference services for CPU-only environments with explicit hardware assumptions, real fallbacks, and predictable degradation.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Not every deployment target has a dedicated accelerator. In many environments, the only safe assumption is a general-purpose CPU. Treating that as a deliberate design constraint makes the service easier to deploy, explain, and operate.

aceu-edge-infer is a small CPU-first inference demo with a documented OpenVINO runtime path. Its ACE-U outputs are illustrative—not a validated assessment of people. The design lesson is broader: state the hardware contract and make the service’s behavior when that contract is not met explicit.

Document the hardware contract

Say which device is required and what is optional. If CPU-only execution is supported, describe the expected model format, available runtime, resource needs, and what performance behavior users should plan for. If an accelerator is optional, list supported devices and the path selected when one is missing.

Make device selection explicit

For an OpenVINO model intended for CPU execution, specify the device in the compile call rather than relying on a default selection:

import openvino as ov

core = ov.Core()
model = core.read_model("models/aceu_ir.xml")
compiled_model = core.compile_model(model, "CPU")

Test the exact runtime package and operating system you plan to ship. If startup cannot load the model or compile it for CPU, do not report the service as ready.

Distinguish a fallback from a failure

A fallback is a real, tested alternative execution path. It may be a different model artifact, a portable runtime, or a slower implementation that produces valid outputs. If none exists, the honest response to a missing runtime is a clear startup failure or an unavailable response—not placeholder scores or a “fallback” label that hides the problem.

Expose execution metadata that helps operators understand the path without leaking environment details:

execution_info = {
    "device": "CPU",
    "precision": "INT8",
    "fallback_used": False,
}

In a real service, derive these values from the compiled model and request path; do not hard-code them when the runtime can choose a different path.

Degrade predictably on constrained hardware

Assume memory and CPU shares may be limited. Measure the model’s memory footprint and end-to-end latency on the target class of device. Start with conservative concurrency; more threads do not automatically mean better p95 latency. If the service supports it, adjust batch size, request timeout, or concurrency by deployment profile, and document the effect.

Do not silently lower quality when the machine is under pressure. If a request is rejected, deferred, or routed to a different precision, make the behavior observable and keep the response contract clear.

Separate startup, readiness, and liveness

  • Startup: load the model and confirm the selected CPU runtime can compile it.
  • Readiness: confirm the service can complete the critical inference path before it receives traffic.
  • Liveness: use a cheap check for a process that is stuck, not an expensive inference on every probe.

A stricter readiness check may delay the first “ready” signal. That is preferable to routing requests to a service that has not loaded its model. Keep checks bounded so probes do not become a source of load.

Keep operational assumptions beside the code

Add a “Hardware assumptions” section to the README and link it from deployment instructions. Include supported devices, runtime versions, precision choices, resource settings, fallback behavior, health endpoints, and a short way to verify the selected execution mode. The next engineer should not have to infer these from source code.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • CPU portability vs. latency: a CPU path broadens where the service can run, but may not meet a workload’s latency target. Measure before promising an SLA.
  • Optional accelerators vs. maintenance: each extra path adds test and support cost; add only devices the product needs.
  • Strict readiness vs. quick deployment: waiting for a successful model load delays traffic, but avoids a false-green service.

Common failures include assuming hardware that is not present, retrying device selection in a tight loop, and leaving hardware requirements undocumented. Provide a clear failure state and a controlled recovery path instead.

Try it yourself

  1. Write the CPU and optional accelerator requirements in your README.
  2. Expose the actual device and precision selected for each execution path.
  3. Simulate a missing optimized runtime and verify that the service fails clearly or uses a genuine tested fallback.
  4. Measure memory and latency under representative CPU limits before selecting concurrency defaults.

Closing thought

Designing for CPU-only execution is not a claim that CPU is always enough. It is a way to make assumptions visible, provide a credible fallback where one exists, and keep the service predictable on the hardware it supports.

Further reading

  • OpenVINO CPU device documentation
  • OpenVINO performance hints and inference optimization
  • OpenVINO model conversion and runtime loading

atom:entry.atom:title: Flaky Tests Are a Concurrency Bug: Fixing Shared State Under Parallel Execution
atom:entry.atom:summary: Flaky tests often signal shared state bugs. Learn to diagnose parallel execution issues, isolate fixtures, and design for deterministic test behavior.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I’ve watched teams chase “test runner bugs” while the real culprit was design. Flakiness is often a concurrency issue—shared mutable state under parallel execution. JUnit 5 can run tests concurrently, so fixtures that share mutable state can make failures appear intermittent. Creating isolated data per test makes the behavior easier to reproduce and diagnose.

The failure mode

You enable parallel test execution and see intermittent failures: “record not found” or “unexpected duplicate.” You re-run and it passes. Blaming the test runner is easy. The problem is shared state: two tests reading/writing the same fixture or relying on an implicit order.

What I learned

Default to per-test fixtures

Use per-test initialization to avoid shared mutable state. In JUnit 5, keep your test instance lifecycle at PER_METHOD and recreate fixtures for each test. If the fixture is expensive, consider a template with parameterization that still isolates state.

Example setup

import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_METHOD)
class EvidenceServiceTest {
private InMemoryStore store;
private EvidenceService service;
@BeforeEach
void init() {
store = new InMemoryStore(); // new store per test
service = new EvidenceService(store);
store.seedProfile("alice", syntheticProfileAlice());
}
@Test
void returnsMissingWhenTimeout() {
// ...
}
@Test
void returnsUnverifiableOnExceptions() {
// ...
}
}

Avoid static mutable fields—especially in helpers

Static caches and helpers make tests faster locally but brittle in parallel. If you truly need a cache, scope it per test, or guard it with thread-safe constructs and clear it explicitly. Better: don’t cache at all in tests unless you benchmarked the need.

Make isolation visible—name-bound fixtures

If a test seeds data, bind it to a unique key per test. Use random UUIDs or test names in keys to prevent accidental cross-test reuse. With Testcontainers, create per-test containers when state isolation is critical; share containers only for read-only tests.

Parallel execution deserves explicit design

JUnit 5 lets you run tests in parallel. That doesn’t mean every test should be parallel. Annotate classes that require single-thread execution, but treat that as a last resort. Prefer making tests parallel-safe by design.

JUnit configuration (illustrative):

junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.enabled = true
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.default = concurrent
junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default = concurrent

Deterministic time and waiting

Tests that sleep and “hope the system is ready” fail under parallel runs. Replace sleeps with explicit synchronization: await a condition, poll with a small backoff, or use latches. Keep timeouts small and deterministic.

Embrace “given-when-then” with isolated builders

Build input data per test with dedicated builders. Don’t reuse a mutable “default profile” object across tests; copy or reconstruct it. Records help: immutable inputs prevent accidental mutation.

Diagnose with logging and seeds

When a test fails intermittently, print seeds and keys that identify data. If you see the same key in two tests, you found shared state. If you see non-deterministic ordering in a collection, sort inputs or assert set equivalence rather than list order.

Per-test container with unique data

class StoreTests {
    private PostgreSQLContainer<?> database;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        database = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:alpine")
            .withDatabaseName("test_" + UUID.randomUUID())
            .withUsername("user")
            .withPassword("test-only");
        database.start();
    }

    @AfterEach
    void tearDown() {
        database.stop();
    }
}

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Isolation vs speed: Per-test fixtures are slower than shared ones. Optimize later—start with correct behavior and only share read-only fixtures.

Parallelism vs determinism: Parallel runs surface concurrency bugs but may require more careful test design. The benefits outweigh the cost.

Container lifecycle vs developer ergonomics: Per-test containers are robust but slower. Consider class-level containers for read-only tests with clear resets.

Failure modes

“Hidden globals”

A helper modifies a static map. Under parallel, tests interleave and fail intermittently.

“Order assumptions”: Tests rely on iteration order of sets or maps; parallel runs expose different orders.

“Implicit sleeps”: Tests use fixed sleeps; faster/slower environments cause out-of-order expectations.

Try it yourself

Switch to PER_METHOD lifecycle and remove static mutable fields in tests. Add unique keys per test to seed data. Enable parallel execution and watch for failures that indicate hidden shared state.

Replace sleep-based readiness with explicit condition checks. Add timeouts and backoff policies.

Document which tests are parallel-safe and why; make non-parallel tests the exception and note the reason.

Further reading

  • JUnit 5 parallel execution
  • Testcontainers for Java

atom:entry.atom:title: Minimal Java container on OCI with TLS to DB
atom:entry.atom:summary: A small, locked-down Java service on an Ampere A1 instance, talking to Oracle Database over TLS.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

I wanted the smallest useful baseline: a Java service in a container, on a cheap OCI instance, connecting to an Oracle database over TLS, with no credentials baked into the image. It should be small enough to read in one sitting and safe enough to build on.

Options and trade-offs

  • Ampere A1 with Podman: efficient and economical, and you need arm64 images.
  • Docker on an x86 shape: the widest image support, at a higher cost as you scale.
  • TLS only versus mTLS with a wallet: TLS means less to handle, and mTLS gives stronger assurance.

My recommendation

For a small service I use an Ampere A1 instance with Podman, TLS first, and mTLS when policy requires it. The image holds only the application. Credentials and any wallet are injected when the container starts. UCP stays at conservative sizes.

Worked example

Install the container tooling on Oracle Linux 8 and build on the same architecture you will run on. Building on the A1 instance avoids cross-architecture surprises.

sudo dnf module install -y container-tools:ol8
sudo dnf install -y podman-docker git

A Dockerfile that runs as a non-root user. The Temurin JRE image is published for arm64 as well as x86.

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre
RUN useradd --system --no-create-home appuser
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/app.jar /app/app.jar
USER appuser
CMD ["java", "-jar", "/app/app.jar"]

Run it with the password supplied as a Podman secret, and with a read-only filesystem and no extra capabilities:

printf '%s' "$DB_PASSWORD" | podman secret create db_password -
 
podman run -d --name app -p 8080:8080 \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop=ALL \
  --env JDBC_URL='<tcps_jdbc_url>' --env DB_USER='<db_user>' \
  --secret db_password,type=env,target=DB_PASSWORD \
  <region-key>.ocir.io/<tenancy-namespace>/myteam/myapp:1.4.2

In the application, build the pool from environment values and keep the sizes modest:

PoolDataSource pds = PoolDataSourceFactory.getPoolDataSource();
pds.setConnectionFactoryClassName("oracle.jdbc.pool.OracleDataSource");
pds.setURL(System.getenv("JDBC_URL"));          // tcps:// URL
pds.setUser(System.getenv("DB_USER"));
pds.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));
pds.setMinPoolSize(2);
pds.setMaxPoolSize(10);
pds.setValidateConnectionOnBorrow(true);

For mTLS, mount the wallet directory read-only at run time, set TNS_ADMIN to it, and let ojdbc.properties supply the wallet location. Do not copy it into the image. Remember to open the application port in both the instance firewall and the network security group.

Checklist

  1. Confirm every dependency and base image supports arm64.
  2. Run as a non-root user with a read-only filesystem.
  3. Inject database credentials at start-up from a secret store.
  4. Start with TLS, and move to mTLS when required.
  5. Size the pool for the database, not for the instance.
  6. Test a bad certificate and a database restart before cutover.

Where this doesn't apply

Large frameworks with big memory footprints may be a poor fit for a small instance. Pick a shape for the workload instead of forcing it onto the smallest one.

One honest limitation

TLS and wallet problems tend to show up as vague connection errors. I keep a tiny test program that only opens a connection, so I can separate driver and certificate problems from application bugs.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Deploying Java Applications on Ampere A1
  • Podman Documentation: podman secret and podman run
  • Oracle JDBC Developer's Guide: Client-Side Security Features

atom:entry.atom:title: Virtual Threads Changed My Mental Model: Practical Lessons From I/O Fan-Out
atom:entry.atom:summary: Virtual threads simplify I/O fan-out. Learn practical lessons: structured fan-out, back pressure, blocking calls, failure handling, and realistic expectations.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Virtual threads changed how I design I/O fan-out in Java services. As an engineering manager who grew up with fixed thread pools, queue sizing, and saturation metrics, I had muscle memory: “pick a pool size, tune it, protect it.” With virtual threads, I can treat blocking I/O more like straightforward code again—without tying throughput to a small pool.

The failure mode

A caller triggers N downstream calls per request (fan-out). With a fixed pool, saturation appears quickly under spikes; with virtual threads, spikes are absorbed but not eliminated. If you translate “we can spawn thousands of threads” into “we don’t need back pressure,” you’ll rediscover failures—just in different places.

What I learned

Think “task-per-thread” for blocking I/O, not “pool-per-service”

Virtual threads make “one virtual thread per blocking task” feasible. You can write linear code for a downstream call and not contort it into callbacks just to avoid blocking. That simplifies failure handling and resource cleanup.

Example fan-out

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Callable<EvidenceResult>> tasks = sources.stream()
        .map(source -> (Callable<EvidenceResult>) source::fetchEvidence)
        .toList();
    List<Future<EvidenceResult>> futures = executor.invokeAll(tasks);
    List<EvidenceResult> results = new ArrayList<>(futures.size());
    for (Future<EvidenceResult> future : futures) {
        results.add(future.get());
    }
    return aggregate(results);
}

This reads like blocking I/O because it is—but with virtual threads, the scheduler multiplexes them efficiently.

Back pressure still matters

If downstream services or data sources choke under spikes, virtual threads won’t magically fix it. The caller can spin up many virtual threads, but the destination still has limits. You need timeouts, rate limits, and circuit breakers. You also need to avoid accidental fan-in (e.g., mass aggregation that blocks on slowest responders indefinitely).

CPU-bound work belongs elsewhere

Virtual threads help with blocking I/O, not CPU-heavy tasks. If a task saturates CPU, the scheduler can’t help—you need to bound parallelism with a platform-appropriate mechanism (e.g., a limited executor or structured concurrency approach) to avoid oversubscription.

Failure semantics are simpler when code is linear

Exception handling in “straight-line” code is clearer than in callback-based designs. You still need to decide whether partial evidence returns a partial result (with Missing/Unverifiable states) or you fail the whole request. Virtual threads don’t make that decision; they just make the code easier to read.

“Thousands of threads” doesn’t mean “no limits”

Virtual threads are cheap, but not free. Sockets, file descriptors, and memory buffers are finite. The OS still enforces resource ceilings. Guard your fan-out with sensible limits: per-request caps, per-destination timeouts, and global safety checks.

Observability shifts upstream

With fixed pools, saturation appears as queue wait time. With virtual threads, saturation shifts to downstream latency and timeouts. Make sure your metrics capture per-destination latency percentiles and error rates. A spike in virtual-thread creation can be fine if destinations are healthy; it’s not fine if percentiles explode.

Test under synthetic spike and tail latency

I haven’t yet measured performance between virtual threads and a fixed pool for the demo. What I do measure is behavior under artificial spikes: do timeouts fire? Does the aggregation return timely partial results with Missing/Unverifiable? Tests simulate slow destinations and verify we don’t hang.

Timeout per downstream call

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<EvidenceResult> future = executor.submit(source::fetch);
    try {
        return future.get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    } catch (TimeoutException timeoutError) {
        future.cancel(true);
        return EvidenceResult.unavailable("timeout");
    }
}

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Simplicity vs explicit limits: Virtual threads reduce boilerplate, but you still must implement back pressure. Silent defaults can mask saturation until it’s too late.

“Everything virtual” vs CPU realities: Virtual threads help with I/O. For CPU-bound work, a bounded executor or workload partitioning is safer.

Observability differences: You lose fixed-pool queue metrics and gain per-destination latency metrics. Update dashboards and alerts accordingly.

Failure modes

“Soft hangs”: Aggregation waits on the slowest responder forever. Add timeouts and partial-return logic.

“Resource leaks”: Thousands of virtual threads keep sockets open longer than intended. Validate resource cleanup paths.

“Oversubscription”: CPU-heavy tasks in virtual threads degrade the whole process. Bound CPU parallelism explicitly.

Try it yourself

Replace a fixed thread pool fan-out with newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() and add per-destination timeouts. Observe behavior under synthetic spikes.

Add aggregation logic that treats timeouts as Missing and downstream errors as Unverifiable. Verify exhaustive handling with pattern matching.

Measure throughput and p95 latency in a controlled environment to inform whether virtual threads help your workload.

Further reading

  • Virtual Threads (JEP 444)
  • Java 21 ExecutorService API

atom:entry.atom:title: Logs, metrics and trace correlation for a Java service in a container
atom:entry.atom:summary: A small set of habits that make a containerised Java service observable without drowning in log volume or metric cost.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Logs, metrics and traces are three different tools, and they only help in an incident when they can be tied together. The common failure is not the lack of data. It is that the data is unstructured, expensive, or impossible to connect to a single request. Containers add a convention on top: write to standard output, and let the platform collect it. Everything else is about keeping that stream useful and cheap.

Options and trade-offs

  • Plain-text logs written to files: easy at first, but hard to parse, and the files fill the container's disk.
  • Structured JSON logs on standard output: parseable, collected by the platform, and the right default.
  • Tracing everything: great detail, but the CPU and storage bill grows with traffic. Sampling keeps the cost predictable.

My recommendation

Log structured JSON to standard output with a small, fixed set of fields. Put a correlation ID on every request at the edge and carry it through the logs. Keep metric labels low cardinality, and sample traces. Alert on user-facing symptoms, not on every raw number.

Worked example

A servlet filter that makes sure every request has a correlation ID, puts it in the logging context, and returns it to the caller.

import jakarta.servlet.*;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import org.slf4j.MDC;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.UUID;

public class CorrelationFilter implements Filter {
    private static final String HEADER = "X-Correlation-Id";

    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        String id = ((HttpServletRequest) req).getHeader(HEADER);
        if (id == null || id.isBlank() || id.length() > 64) {
            id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        }
        MDC.put("correlation_id", id);
        ((HttpServletResponse) res).setHeader(HEADER, id);
        try {
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } finally {
            MDC.remove("correlation_id");
        }
    }
}

The Logback configuration that writes each event as one JSON line to standard output, including the correlation ID from the MDC. It uses the open-source Logstash encoder.

<configuration>
  <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder"/>
  </appender>
  <root level="INFO">
    <appender-ref ref="STDOUT"/>
  </root>
</configuration>

Then log with parameters, so nothing is formatted when the level is off:

log.info("request_finished route={} status={} durationMs={}", route, status, elapsedMs);
log.warn("upstream_failed upstream={} reason={}", "inventory", "timeout");

Checklist

  1. Log JSON to standard output, with level, timestamp, component, message and correlation ID.
  2. Create the correlation ID at the edge, accept a sane inbound one, and cap its length.
  3. Keep metric labels to a small set such as route class and outcome, never per user.
  4. Sample traces, and raise the rate temporarily during an incident.
  5. Alert on error rate and latency, and link the alert to a dashboard or runbook.

Where this doesn't apply

A single small service may not need distributed tracing at all. Structured logs with a correlation ID will already answer most questions.

One honest limitation

Observability has a cost. Every extra log line and span uses CPU and memory, and during an incident, noisy logging can make the incident worse.

Sources

  • SLF4J Manual: Mapped Diagnostic Context (MDC)
  • Logback Documentation: Appenders
  • OpenTelemetry Documentation: Sampling
  • Docker Docs: View container logs

atom:entry.atom:title: Triage Without Burning Out: Sustainable Patterns for Issues and PRs
atom:entry.atom:summary: Reduce burnout with sustainable triage: clear labels, response-time placeholders, friendly declines, and contributor pathways you can maintain.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Maintaining an open-source project alongside a full-time job means learning to triage sustainably. You can’t answer everything immediately or accept every idea. You can design labeling and response patterns that make your limited time effective — and that keep contributors engaged without exhausting you.

The failure mode

You wake up to ten new issues and three PRs. Two are duplicates, three ask for features outside the project scope, and several lack context. You try to answer quickly and get pulled into long threads that don’t move the project forward. A week later, you’re behind, less responsive, and a contributor feels ignored.

What I learned

Label early, label consistently

Set up labels that reflect workflow, not internal discussions: “good first issue,” “help wanted,” “needs reproduction,” “needs test,” “scope discussion,” “declined” (with a short reason). Use them as soon as you read an issue. Labels create a shared vocabulary and make your backlog scannable.

Response-time expectations reduce anxiety

State response-time expectations publicly: for example, “New issues are triaged within two business days; PR reviews are typically completed within one week.” Adjust those targets to fit your team. If you’re out-of-office, post a brief note in Discussions or the README. Contributors appreciate clarity.

Friendly declines are a kindness — write them well

Declining an idea is not rejecting a person. Use a short, warm template that explains scope, suggests alternatives, and invites contribution along defined paths (e.g., plugins rather than core changes). Label the issue “declined” and close it with the message.

Decline template

Thanks for the idea! For now, this is out of scope for the project.

We’re keeping the core lean and recommending plugins for extensions.

If you’d like to explore it as a plugin, happy to provide a template link.

Require minimal tests, not maximal rigor

For small projects, a minimal test required by the PR template keeps quality up without deterring contributors. Tests should be fast, easy to write, and close to the code change. If a PR lacks tests, add a gentle reminder and label “needs test.”

Batch reviews and avoid context switching

Schedule triage windows — twice a week, for example. Batch issue labeling and PR reviews in those windows. It reduces context switching and lets contributors anticipate when they’ll hear back. If needed, add a triage bot that labels based on keywords to reduce manual work.

Document “how to get a fast review”

Spell out what gets fast attention: small PRs with tests, clean diffs, and narrow scope; issues with reproductions and logs; ideas aligned with plugin paths. Encourage contributors to write “before/after” summaries in PR descriptions and to link to the relevant part of the code.

Track your backlog and set a capacity

If too many issues pile up, prune. Close old issues that lack detail after a friendly ping. Move discussions into one “scope discussion” thread for big feature ideas. Keep your backlog reasonable and honest about capacity.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Strict labels vs flexibility: Rules reduce effort but can feel rigid. Counterbalance with friendly messages and occasional exceptions.

Minimal tests vs depth: Minimal tests ensure basic correctness; complex changes may need deeper coverage. Ask for more when a change warrants it.

Batch triage vs real-time responsiveness: Batching reduces burnout; some contributors prefer faster feedback. Make expectations explicit.

Failure modes

“Unlabeled backlog”: Issues pile up without labels; you forget context. Solution: label on first read.

“Harsh declines”

A terse “no” closes doors. Solution: a kind template that suggests plugin paths or future reconsideration.

“Hidden OOO”: You vanish for a week without notice; contributors lose trust. Solution: brief status notes when you’re unavailable.

Try it yourself

Create and apply a lightweight label set. Add “good first issue” and curate five tasks.

Publish response-time expectations

and measure response times over the next month.

Adopt a friendly decline template and a short “how to get a fast review” section in CONTRIBUTING.md.

Further reading

  • GitHub Docs: Issue and pull request templates
  • GitHub Docs: Community health files

atom:entry.atom:title: Verifiable Doesn’t Mean Verified: Getting Issuer, Holder, and Verifier Right
atom:entry.atom:summary: Verifiable credentials can be signed and valid yet still wrong. Learn issuer/holder/verifier roles, failure modes, and checks beyond JSON and signatures.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I’m an engineering manager with experience integrating identity-verification flows conceptually aligned with Microsoft Entra Verified ID. One habit that keeps teams honest is repeating the phrase: verifiable doesn’t mean verified. The W3C Verifiable Credentials data model makes claims portable and cryptographically provable, but it doesn’t magically make those claims true, up to date, or appropriate for your use case.

The failure mode

A team builds a credential verifier that checks JSON shape and a signature. The code reports “valid.” A downstream feature treats the claim as true. Weeks later, someone discovers the issuer did, in fact, sign the credential, but the subject was not the person currently presenting it, or the credential expired months ago. The failure wasn’t cryptography; it was process: treating “verifiable” as “verified.”

What I learned

Roles and responsibilities: issuer, holder, verifier

Issuer: Asserts something about a subject (the holder) and signs the assertion. Their trustworthiness is a human, contractual, and policy question, not a purely technical one.
Holder: Receives and stores the credential; presents it to a verifier. Binding the holder to the subject of the credential (is this person who the claim describes?) is a separate step.
Verifier: Evaluates signature validity, checks schema, ensures the issuer is trusted for that claim type, confirms the subject binding, interprets policy (expiry, audience, revocation), and decides whether to accept the claim.

Well-formed is necessary but not sufficient

A credential can be:

Well-formed: It conforms to expected JSON structure.
Signed: The cryptographic proof validates against the issuer’s public key.
Trusted: The issuer is recognized and allowed to assert this particular claim type.
Bound: The subject is provably the presenter.
Current: It hasn’t expired and isn’t revoked. Only when all are satisfied does “valid” approach “usable.”

Separate signature validation from trust decision

Cryptography answers “did the claimed issuer sign this payload?” Trust answers “do we trust this issuer for this claim type right now?” You need both. If the issuer isn’t in your trust registry for the claim being evaluated, the result shouldn’t be “invalid claim,” it should be “untrusted issuer for this policy.”

Subject binding is a first-class step

A classic failure mode: someone presents a signed credential about a subject, but the presenter isn’t the subject. In practical flows, the verifier should confirm that the presenter’s wallet or identity key pair matches the credential subject, or use an out-of-band binding method aligned with your policy. If binding is missing, treat the result as “unverifiable” rather than “false.”

Expiry and audience are policy gates, not parsing details

Expiry and audience are part of the claim semantics. A credential can be signed and well-formed yet expired (or intended for a different audience). These conditions should result in “policy failure” states distinct from “cryptographic failure.”

Revocation closes the loop

Issuance is easy; ensuring the claim is still valid is the hard part. Revocation checks must avoid “phone home” privacy leaks (more in the revocation article below). Even a toy system benefits from an offline revocation list or privacy-preserving status check.

Distinguish “invalid” from “unverifiable”

Illustrative verification flow

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Literal

Status = Literal["accepted", "unverifiable", "invalid"]

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ValidationResult:
    signature_valid: bool
    issuer_trusted: bool
    subject_bound: bool
    policy_ok: bool
    status: Status

# Keep proof validation, issuer trust, subject binding, and policy checks separate.
# The exact proof checks depend on the credential format and verifier library supported by the deployment.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Strict policy gates vs user friction: Strong audience/expiry checks reduce misuse but can frustrate users who present slightly out-of-date credentials. The fix is short-lived credentials and good UX.

Offline trust lists vs dynamic fetch: Offline lists avoid privacy leaks but risk staleness. Consider periodic sync with no per-verification lookups.

Subject binding rigor vs simplicity: Strong binding reduces fraud but adds ceremony. Pick the approach that fits your risk.

Failure modes

“Signed, therefore true”: Conflating cryptographic validity with trust. Fix by separating proof validation from issuer trust policy.

“Presenter ≠ subject”: Accepting credentials without subject binding. Fix by explicit binding checks.

“Policy drift”: Undocumented audience/expiry rules. Fix with centralized policy and tests.

Try it yourself

Implement a verifier that separately evaluates cryptographic proof, issuer trust, subject binding, and policy gates.

Return “unverifiable” for missing binding and “invalid” for failed policy (e.g., expiry).

Measure performance across well-formed accepts vs policy failures to understand user impact.

Further reading

  • W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0
  • Microsoft Entra Verified ID verification planning
  • Configure a Verified ID verifier

atom:entry.atom:title: Don’t Ship What You Haven’t Scanned: Gating Images Before Production
atom:entry.atom:summary: Build an SBOM, scan each container image, and gate releases on actionable vulnerability severity.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Images move quickly; vulnerability information changes just as quickly. My baseline is straightforward: make image contents visible, scan before release, gate on actionable findings, and define a narrow exception path with an owner and an expiry.

This is not a claim that scanners make an image safe. A scan is one control in a larger process. The goal is to replace last-minute surprises with a repeatable decision before an image reaches production.

Start with an inventory

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) lists software components included in an image. Generating one during the build gives scanners and reviewers a concrete inventory to inspect. Docker Buildx can attach an SBOM attestation to an image:

# Build and push to a registry so the SBOM attestation travels with the image.
docker buildx build \
  --tag "$IMAGE" \
  --sbom=true \
  --push .

Build attestations depend on the BuildKit builder and where the image is stored. Verify that the registry contains the SBOM and that your scanner can read it; do not assume a successful command means the inventory is being retained in the place you expect.

Gate on findings the team can act on

Pick a severity policy and make it a failing CI step. For example, Trivy can return a non-zero exit status when High or Critical findings are present:

# IMAGE is the exact tag or digest built by the preceding step.
trivy image \
  --exit-code 1 \
  --severity HIGH,CRITICAL \
  "$IMAGE"

Choose policy with the people who own the service. Severity labels are useful triage signals, but they do not tell you whether a vulnerable code path is reachable in your application. Prioritize fixable findings; keep visibility into the rest and record remediation plans.

Make exceptions narrow and temporary

Sometimes a scanner reports a finding with no available fix, or a team can show that a vulnerable path is not reachable in its deployment. If your policy allows an exception, require at least:

  • a named owner responsible for revisiting it;
  • a short technical justification and the affected image digest;
  • a remediation plan or a reason no fix is available;
  • an expiry date that triggers re-review.

An exception should have an end. An expired exception returns to the gate for a fresh decision.

Scan third-party images and every release candidate

Review a base image or build tool before first use, prefer trustworthy publishers, and record the digest of the image you evaluated. Scan the image that will actually be released, not only the Dockerfile or an earlier local build. Repeat the scan when rebuilding because packages and advisories change.

Treat scanner failures as operational failures

Scanning can fail because a registry is unavailable, an advisory feed cannot be fetched, a token expired, or the runner ran out of disk. These states are different from “the scan completed and found a vulnerability.” Preserve enough CI status and logs to tell which happened, and make sure infrastructure errors cannot turn into a silent pass.

Keep the gate fast enough to keep

If every scan takes too long, teams will look for ways around it. Cache what is safe to cache, tune the scanner, and make results easy to understand—but do not quietly skip scanning for small code changes. Also record who approved exceptions and when; keep logs free of credentials and other secrets.

Failure modes to test

  • The gate reports but does not block: test the pipeline with a known finding and confirm the build fails.
  • Advisory access expires: make registry or scanner authentication failures visible and blocking.
  • The SBOM is missing: treat a missing expected artifact as a failed build, not an empty inventory.
  • A clean scan becomes stale: rebuild and rescan as dependencies or vulnerability data change.

Try it in your pipeline

  1. Generate an SBOM for each release image and verify that it is retained.
  2. Run a vulnerability scan on the exact image tag or digest that will ship.
  3. Set a failing threshold, such as High and Critical, with a written exception policy.
  4. Keep scanner outages separate from vulnerability findings in the CI result.

Closing thought

A scan is most useful when it changes a release decision. Make image contents visible, agree on what blocks a release, and give every exception an owner and a clock.

Further reading

  • Docker SBOM attestations
  • Docker SBOM and provenance attestations in GitHub Actions
  • Trivy severity filtering and exit codes

atom:entry.atom:title: Semantic Versioning Is a Promise, Not a Formality
atom:entry.atom:summary: SemVer is a user promise. Learn to recognize breaking changes, communicate them, write migration notes, and keep releases predictable for small projects.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Semantic Versioning (SemVer) looks straightforward: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. In practice, the hardest part is deciding when a change is breaking. In a small project, breaking changes cost contributors time and confidence. They also generate extra triage work you don’t have time for. For a public API, SemVer is a promise: when a contract change requires action from users, communicate it clearly and choose the appropriate version increment.

The failure mode

You change an endpoint’s response shape from {type:"present"} to {status:"present"} and add a field. Tests in your project pass because you updated them. A user’s integration breaks silently because they were parsing the old field. You release as a minor bump. Issues pile up. SemVer wasn’t just a label; it was a promise you broke.

What I learned

Define “breaking” for your project — then honor it

For a public API, breaking means any change that requires user action. That includes renames, removals, default behavior changes, stricter validation, and shifts in documented semantics. For plugin contracts, it includes method signatures and return-object fields. Write this down in CONTRIBUTING.md or RELEASE.md.

Use PATCH for fixes, MINOR for additive changes, MAJOR for breaking

PATCH: bug fixes that don’t change behavior or contracts. MINOR: new additive features, fields, or optional paths that don’t require code changes from users. MAJOR: anything else. If in doubt, lean toward stricter classification — small projects benefit from conservative signaling.

Keep a changelog that’s useful, not performative

A good CHANGELOG.md lists new features, fixes, and breaking changes with clear “migration” steps. Link to PRs and discussions when helpful, but don’t drown readers in noise. Make breaking changes a dedicated section with bullet points and example code.

Changelog entry (example)

## [2.0.0] - 2026-02-15
### Breaking
- Plugin interface: `evaluate()` return now requires `score_delta`.
- API response: field `note` renamed to `message`.
- Migration:
  - Plugins: provide a score delta when constructing the result.
  - Clients: read the renamed message field.
### Added
- New synthetic evidence source: "activity_count".
### Fixed
- Corrected null-handling in JSON serialization for missing evidence.

Automate release notes and tags, but write the words yourself

Automated release workflows help: tag versions, publish notes, and attach artifacts. The content of the notes should be authored by you or a maintainer who understands the changes. Meaningful context beats auto-generated lists.

Communicate before you break

— deprecation notes and timelines If you plan a breaking change, announce it with a deprecation note. Add warnings to logs, include a deprecation section in the changelog, and post a short explanation in discussions. Offer a migration window (e.g., two minor releases) and stick to it.

Validate SemVer behavior with contract tests

Combine SemVer discipline with tests: run a suite that loads the previous minor version’s contracts against the new release where feasible. If tests fail because you changed behavior without bumping MAJOR, you’ll catch it before publishing.

Keep scope under control

— fewer breaking changes, batched when necessary Batch breaking changes into a single major release rather than sprinkling them across minors. This helps users plan upgrades and reduces your triage load. Once you ship a major, leave a quiet window before the next one.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Strict SemVer vs development speed: Bumping MAJOR and writing migration notes take time. They also save user time and reduce issue volume.

Deprecation windows vs maintenance overhead: Supporting old paths gives contributors time to adapt. For small projects, choose short, firm windows.

Automated release processes vs human judgment: Automation speeds delivery; human-curated notes ensure clarity. Pair them.

Failure modes

“Silent breaking minor”: Change that requires user action shipped as MINOR. It erodes trust and increases support requirements.

“Vague changelog”: Readers can’t tell what changed. Solution: explicit “Breaking,” “Added,” “Fixed” sections with migration steps.

“SemVer theater”: You declare SemVer, then ignore it in practice. Users stop trusting your version signals. Solution: define rules and follow them.

Try it yourself

Write a short “What counts as breaking” policy tailored to your project and add it to CONTRIBUTING.md.

Adopt Keep a Changelog structure and commit to explicit migration notes for breaking changes.

Add a contract test suite that runs compatibility checks against the previous minor version. If it fails, reconsider your classification.

Further reading

  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0
  • Keep a Changelog
  • GitHub Docs: Managing releases

atom:entry.atom:title: OCIR basics: push/pull, private repos, auth tokens
atom:entry.atom:summary: The registry commands I actually run, and the small details that cause most login failures.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Registry (OCIR) is simple once you know the rules, and confusing until then. Most failures come from the same few places: a wrong region endpoint, a wrong username format, or an expired token.

I wanted a short reference that gets a private repository working and keeps it private.

Options and trade-offs

  • Public repositories: easy to share, and only suitable for images that are safe for anyone to pull.
  • Private repositories with auth tokens: the standard approach, and it needs good token hygiene.
  • Short-lived or bearer-style credentials: possible for pipelines, with more setup to maintain.

My recommendation

Use private repositories and user auth tokens. Create the repository explicitly in the compartment that owns it, instead of letting a first push create it. Keep the regional endpoint and the username format written down where the team can find them.

Worked example

Log in with the registry endpoint for your region. The username begins with your tenancy namespace. If your user belongs to a non-default identity domain or is federated, the username format changes, so check the documentation for your case.

docker login <region-key>.ocir.io
# Username: <tenancy-namespace>/<username>
# Password: <auth-token>
 
oci artifacts container repository create \
  --compartment-id <compartment_ocid> \
  --display-name myteam/myapp \
  --is-public false
 
docker tag myapp:1.4.2 <region-key>.ocir.io/<tenancy-namespace>/myteam/myapp:1.4.2
docker push <region-key>.ocir.io/<tenancy-namespace>/myteam/myapp:1.4.2

And the policies, kept separate for people who browse and people who manage:

Allow group image-viewers to inspect repos in tenancy
Allow group image-publishers to manage repos in compartment registry

I tag with a version, not latest, so a rollback is a one-line change. A user can hold only a small number of auth tokens, so plan token replacement for your pipelines before it is urgent.

Checklist

  1. Know the endpoint for your region and use it consistently.
  2. Use the tenancy namespace in the username, and the auth token as the password.
  3. Create repositories explicitly and confirm they are private.
  4. Set separate policies for viewing and managing repositories.
  5. Tag images with versions, and avoid latest in production.
  6. Set a retention rule, and watch pulls for surprises.

Where this doesn't apply

Air-gapped clusters cannot reach OCIR directly. They need a mirrored or internal registry instead.

One honest limitation

Auth tokens expire or get replaced, and a stale token in a pipeline fails at the worst time. Treat it like any other credential and give it an owner and a rotation date.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Pushing Images Using the Docker CLI
  • OCI Documentation: Logging in to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure Registry
  • OCI Documentation: Required Policies for Container Registry

atom:entry.atom:title: Records Aren’t Just Less Typing: Modeling Ambiguity Without Nulls
atom:entry.atom:summary: Modern Java lets you model ambiguity without nulls. Learn records, sealed interfaces, and pattern matching to represent missing and unverifiable states clearly.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I’m an engineering manager with a background in Java backend systems. One lesson that keeps paying dividends is this: ambiguity deserves types, not comments. Nulls and booleans blur meaning. “false,” “zero,” and “we don’t know” are not interchangeable. With modern Java (records, sealed interfaces, pattern matching), I model uncertainty explicitly and make ambiguity impossible to ignore.

Modern Java can express these outcomes as records and sealed types: Present, Missing, and Unverifiable. The same pattern works in ordinary service domains; it does not depend on a scoring model.

The failure mode

You return a number for a score and a boolean “hasEvidence.” A caller subtracts two scores and treats “0” as “no evidence,” then logs an anomaly when “0” appears alongside “hasEvidence=true.” The model caused this. Nulls and booleans encourage shortcuts and misinterpretation.

What I learned

Use records for immutable, transparent domain data

Records let me define concise, immutable carriers without boilerplate. They encourage a bias toward immutability and make the intent clear.

Example response

public record AceuResponse(
ScoreOrUnknown authenticity,
ScoreOrUnknown credibility,
ScoreOrUnknown empathy,
ScoreOrUnknown uniqueness
) {}
public sealed interface ScoreOrUnknown permits Score, Missing, Unverifiable {}
public record Score(double value) implements ScoreOrUnknown {
public Score {
if (Double.isNaN(value) || value < 0.0 || value > 1.0) {
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Score must be [0,1]");
}
}
}
public record Missing(String reason) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}
public record Unverifiable(String note) implements ScoreOrUnknown {}

Records keep the data small and immutable. The sealed hierarchy enforces the set of states at compile time.

Replace nulls and boolean flags with sealed states

The temptation to use Double/Boolean and encode special states with null or false is strong. Resist it. Sealed interfaces make the valid state space explicit and force exhaustive handling. A boolean can’t distinguish “not applicable,” “not yet computed,” and “calculation failed.”

Use pattern matching for exhaustive case handling

Pattern matching in switch makes code read like the domain. It also turns omissions into compile errors when you use exhaustive switches.

Example handler:

public String render(ScoreOrUnknown s) {
return switch (s) {
case Score sc          -> "score=" + sc.value();
case Missing miss      -> "missing=" + miss.reason();
case Unverifiable unv  -> "unverifiable=" + unv.note();

};

}

By handling each case explicitly, I make it impossible to “forget” one or conflate states.

Prefer intent-rich types over ad-hoc maps and strings

When a state needs more context (e.g., why data is missing), capture it in the type. Missing(String reason) and Unverifiable(String note) beat opaque strings and comments. If callers need to act differently based on the reason, add a reason code enum to the record.

Keep aggregates typed—don’t flatten too early

A response with four dimensions should preserve each dimension’s state. Avoid flattening to a single “overall score.” The minute you collapse, you discard information the caller needs for good decisions. In the demo, each dimension returns a ScoreOrUnknown. Only the caller decides how to combine them, and the compiler forces handling of unknowns.

Embed validation where it belongs

Put invariants in the type’s constructor. Scores are [0,1]; reasons should be concise, not multi-paragraph blobs. Records make these guardrails trivial to implement consistently.

Use test fixtures that exercise every branch

Define parameterized tests for your sealed states. For each dimension, test Score, Missing, and Unverifiable. Assert that pattern matching hits each branch, and that any new state added later causes compilation failures in exhaustive switches until it’s handled.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

More types vs fewer booleans: Sealed types add structure and a few extra classes. The upside is clarity and compile-time enforcement; the downside is minor boilerplate, which records minimize.

Exhaustiveness vs flexibility: Exhaustive switches break on new states until handled. That’s a feature (safety) but can feel strict when you prototype quickly.

Text reasons vs structured codes: Free-form strings are easier; structured enums enable programmatic handling. Choose based on how callers use the data.

Failure modes

“Shadow nulls”

A downstream library returns null and you forget to wrap it in a sealed state. Guard external boundaries with adapters.

“State leakage”: Someone serializes ScoreOrUnknown to a shape that drops the state label (e.g., value=0.0 only). Add JSON configuration that includes a type field and test the wire format.

“Catch-all case”: Using a default branch in pattern matching reintroduces ambiguity. Avoid default; keep exhaustive cases explicit.

Try it yourself

Replace nullable fields for ambiguous states with a sealed interface and record implementations. Add exhaustive pattern matching where you consume them.

Write tests that construct each state per dimension and assert wire-format correctness (e.g., JSON includes the state “type”).

Audit one path where a null sneaks through and add an adapter to convert it into Missing or Unverifiable with a reason code.

Further reading

  • Records (JEP 395)
  • Sealed Classes (JEP 409)
  • Pattern Matching for switch (JEP 441)

atom:entry.atom:title: A Breaking Change in Someone Else’s PR: Guarding Extension Points Without Blocking Contributions
atom:entry.atom:summary: Extension points are fragile. Learn interface versioning, deprecation windows, and contract tests that catch breaking changes in plugin PRs before merge.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Community projects depend on contributions from people who did not write the original code. That openness creates a compatibility challenge: a change can pass local unit tests while still breaking plugins written against the documented interface. Extensibility needs contract tests and clear versioning.

The failure mode

A contributor refactors a plugin interface, renaming a method and changing its return shape. Their tests pass. Your CI passes. You merge. One week later, a different contributor’s PR, built on the previous interface, fails unexpectedly. You didn’t catch the breaking change because you had no compatibility tests enforcing the plugin contract.

What I learned

Treat extension points as public contracts

If you support a plugin API, document it as a minimal, stable contract. Keep it small, reduce optional features, and define explicit versioning. Favor additive changes; avoid changing semantics quietly.

Minimal contract (illustrative)

# your_project/core.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceResult:
type: str  # "present" | "missing" | "unverifiable"
note: str = ""
score_delta: float = 0.0
class EvidenceSource:
name: str
def evaluate(self, profile: dict) -> EvidenceResult:
"""
Input: dictionary of profile fields (synthetic in demo)
Output: EvidenceResult with type, note, and optional score_delta
"""
raise NotImplementedError

Version the interface explicitly

Add an interface version constant in the core module. Plugins import and declare the version they target. CI checks that plugin declarations match the core version and that any bump is accompanied by a deprecation window.

Versioning example:

# your_project/core_version.py
INTERFACE_VERSION = "1.2.0"  # semantic versioned
# plugin declares support
SUPPORTED_VERSIONS = {"1.2.0"}  # plugins can add multiple supported versions

Deprecation windows — commit to dates and behavior When you change the interface, announce deprecations with a grace window: two minor releases or a set number of weeks. During the window, keep the old behavior working and warn at runtime (without breaking tests). At the end, remove the old path and bump the interface version.

Contract tests in CI

Unit tests validate plugin internals. Contract tests validate extension points. Write tests that load every plugin and execute a baseline scenario: call evaluate() with a standard profile, assert return types and fields, and assert compatibility with the current core version. Fail the build on mismatch.

Contract test skeleton:

import importlib

from your_project.core import EvidenceResult
from your_project.core_version import INTERFACE_VERSION

PLUGIN_MODULES = ["your_project.plugins.example_plugin"]

def test_all_plugins_implement_contract():
    for module_name in PLUGIN_MODULES:
        module = importlib.import_module(module_name)
        plugin = module.ExamplePlugin()
        result = plugin.evaluate({"example": True})
        assert isinstance(result, EvidenceResult)
        assert result.status in {"present", "missing", "unverifiable"}
        assert INTERFACE_VERSION in module.SUPPORTED_VERSIONS

Your CI should run both unit and contract tests. If the core changes, test the change against every supported plugin. If external plugins live in separate repositories, publish a small test harness they can add to their own CI.

Communicate interface changes in release notes Semantic version your interface. A breaking change to the plugin API is a major bump. The release notes should list exactly what changed and a minimal migration example. They should also link deprecation windows and final removal dates.

Example release note

## Plugin API 2.0.0 (breaking)
- Keep the result status field unchanged.
- Make the score delta field required.
- Migration: provide a zero delta when a plugin has no score change.
- Publish a deprecation window and removal date.

Keep extension points narrow Every new method or field in a plugin contract increases fragility. Keep it small. If contributors want flexibility, let them model complexity inside their plugin; keep the core contract simple, documented, and testable.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Strict contract tests vs contributor agility: Some contributors will feel slowed by extra checks. Counterbalance with templates and examples.

Deprecation windows vs maintenance overhead: Maintaining old paths for a window adds complexity. Keep windows short and focused for small projects.

Central testing vs distributed plugins

If plugins live elsewhere, you can’t run their tests pre-merge. Provide a harness and encourage adoption.

Failure modes

“Silent break”

A contributor changes the contract; unit tests pass; no compatibility suite fails. Solution: contract tests that load plugins and validate the core expectations.

“Major bump fatigue”: Frequent major bumps erode trust. Solution: batch breaking changes and make additive changes where possible.

“Ambiguous release notes”: Vague notes cause confusion. Solution: concrete migration steps and example code in release notes.

Try it yourself

Add an INTERFACE_VERSION constant and require plugins to declare supported versions.

Implement CI contract tests that import and execute all plugins against the core contract.

Document a deprecation window policy in CONTRIBUTING.md. Commit to timelines and stick to them.

Further reading

  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0
  • Keep a Changelog
  • GitHub Actions: Building and testing

atom:entry.atom:title: Vault + DB wallets: secure distribution patterns (illustrative)
atom:entry.atom:summary: Generating an Autonomous Database wallet, keeping it in Vault, and rebuilding it only where it is needed.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Mutual TLS to Autonomous Database needs a wallet. In practice that wallet ends up in a chat thread, in a repo, or baked into a container image, and rotating it means finding every copy.

I wanted the wallet to have one home, a controlled way out, and a short life on disk.

Options and trade-offs

  • Copying the wallet files around: fast, hard to rotate and hard to audit.
  • Wallet files as Vault secrets: access is governed by IAM and logged. The files need encoding and a rebuild step.
  • Server-authenticated TLS without a wallet: fewer artifacts. It depends on the database allowing TLS connections without mTLS.

My recommendation

Generate the wallet from the database service, store its files as Vault secrets, and let the runtime principal read them at startup. The application recreates the files in a protected directory, sets TNS_ADMIN, and connects through the TNS alias.

Worked example

Generate the wallet and push the files into Vault. The CLI needs base64 content, while the Console encodes plain text for you.

oci db autonomous-database generate-wallet \
  --autonomous-database-id <db_ocid> \
  --file wallet.zip \
  --password "<wallet_password>"
 
unzip wallet.zip -d wallet
base64 -w0 wallet/cwallet.sso > cwallet.sso.b64
 
oci vault secret create-base64 \
  --compartment-id <compartment_ocid> \
  --vault-id <vault_ocid> \
  --key-id <symmetric_key_ocid> \
  --secret-name db_wallet_cwallet_sso \
  --secret-content-content "$(cat cwallet.sso.b64)" \
  --secret-content-stage CURRENT

Repeat for the other files the connection needs, usually tnsnames.ora, sqlnet.ora and ojdbc.properties. At startup, the app reads each secret, decodes it and writes it into a directory only its own user can access. The sketch below shows the permission handling.

Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("wallet",
    PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rwx------")));
for (var e : walletSecrets.entrySet()) {          // name -> base64 content
    Files.write(dir.resolve(e.getKey()), Base64.getDecoder().decode(e.getValue()));
}
// start the JVM or pool with -Doracle.net.tns_admin=<dir> or TNS_ADMIN=<dir>

The ojdbc.properties file that ships in the wallet refers to the TNS_ADMIN directory for its wallet location, so it works unchanged when you rebuild the directory.

Checklist

  1. Generate the wallet from the database service and track when it expires.
  2. Store each file as a secret, using base64 for CLI and API paths.
  3. Give the runtime principal read access to those secrets only.
  4. Rebuild the wallet directory at runtime with owner-only permissions, and never bake it into an image.
  5. Confirm the server certificate name check is on, and log wallet reads.
  6. Keep the previous secret version for a short time in case rotation goes wrong.

Where this doesn't apply

If your policy allows server-authenticated TLS, you may not need a wallet at all. That removes the distribution problem entirely.

One honest limitation

Wallets are multi-file, and the cleanup of temporary files is easy to forget. Test the rebuild path and the deletion path as carefully as the connection itself.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Downloading Client Credentials (Wallets) for Autonomous Database
  • OCI CLI Reference: oci vault secret create-base64
  • OCI Documentation: Connecting with JDBC and a Wallet

atom:entry.atom:title: Container limits and the JVM: why your heap is not your memory limit
atom:entry.atom:summary: A practical look at memory and CPU limits for Java services: sizing the heap, surviving back-pressure and recognising an out-of-memory kill.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Without limits, a hot container can starve its neighbours. With limits that are too tight, it gets killed and restarts in a loop. Either way, the failure spreads: one tier is slow, upstream timeouts fire, retries pile up, and a small problem becomes an outage. On the JVM there is an extra trap. The heap is only part of the memory a process uses. Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache, direct buffers and GC structures all live outside it, so a container limit equal to the heap size is almost guaranteed to be exceeded.

Options and trade-offs

  • No limits: nothing gets killed by the runtime, but one runaway service can degrade the whole host.
  • A hard limit with a fixed -Xmx: predictable, but easy to get wrong when the limit changes and the heap flag does not.
  • A hard limit with a percentage-based heap: the JVM sizes the heap from the container limit, and you leave headroom for everything else.

My recommendation

Set a memory limit, let the JVM size its heap from it with a percentage, and leave real headroom for native memory. Bound every queue so overload becomes a fast, explicit refusal instead of a slow death. Make the out-of-memory case easy to recognise.

Worked example

The Compose file sets the limit and tells the JVM to use 70 percent of it for the heap. The rest is headroom.

services:
  api:
    image: demo/api:1.4.2
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
    environment:
      JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M

A tiny program shows what the JVM actually sees inside the container, which is the first thing to check when sizing goes wrong:

public class WhatDoIHave {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Runtime rt = Runtime.getRuntime();
        System.out.printf("processors=%d maxHeap=%dMB%n",
                rt.availableProcessors(), rt.maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024));
    }
}

For back-pressure, use a bounded queue and refuse work when it is full, instead of accepting everything and falling over later:

import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class BoundedWorkers {
    private final ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
            4, 4, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
            new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100),
            new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());

    /** Returns an HTTP-style status: 202 accepted, 503 over capacity. */
    public int submit(Runnable task) {
        try {
            pool.execute(task);
            return 202;
        } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
            return 503;
        }
    }
}

When a container disappears with exit code 137, check whether the kernel killed it:

docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' api
docker stats --no-stream api

Checklist

  1. Set memory and CPU limits, and write down why each number was chosen.
  2. Use a heap percentage, and leave headroom for native memory.
  3. Bound every queue, and return a clear over-capacity response when it is full.
  4. Log queue depth, rejected work and memory use so the problem is visible before the kill.
  5. Load test with the real limits applied, and watch what the upstream tier does.

Where this doesn't apply

These numbers are starting points for a small service. Large heaps, many threads or heavy direct-buffer use all change the headroom you need, and only measurement on your own workload settles it.

One honest limitation

Limits shrink the blast radius but do not prevent incidents. A service that is out of memory still fails; the point is that it fails predictably and recovers quickly.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Resource constraints
  • Oracle Java Documentation: Java in containers (JVM ergonomics)
  • Docker Docs: docker container inspect

atom:entry.atom:title: Benchmarking Honestly: Building a Repeatable, Trustworthy Inference Benchmark
atom:entry.atom:summary: Build inference benchmarks that report warm-up, latency percentiles, output parity, and hardware conditions.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Benchmarks are easy to fool. Run a handful of requests on a quiet laptop, choose the number that looks good, and almost any model can appear fast. Production has warm-up, load, input variation, and hardware contention. A useful benchmark makes those conditions visible.

In aceu-edge-infer, I keep a small harness that compares FP32 and INT8 inference and records latency and output deltas. The sample inputs are synthetic, so its results are method scaffolding—not evidence of production performance. The measurement discipline is what I want the demo to teach.

Decide what question the benchmark answers

Are you measuring cold start, steady-state single-request latency, or throughput under concurrent work? Those are different measurements. State the workload, model artifact, runtime and device, input shape, batch size, thread/concurrency settings, and whether preprocessing and post-processing are included.

Warm up—and report cold start separately

The first call may include model compilation, memory allocation, cache fill, or runtime initialization. If the question is steady-state latency, run a planned warm-up and keep those samples out of the measured set. If cold start matters to users, report it as its own metric instead of mixing it into steady-state numbers.

Report percentiles as well as averages

Users feel slow requests, not just the mean. Report p50, p95, and p99 latency for each model variant, along with the sample count and run duration. Tail percentiles need enough samples to be meaningful; do not imply precision the benchmark cannot support.

Compare the same inputs and check outputs
