Run the same representative inputs through FP32 and INT8. Compare both the score deltas and task-level decisions. For classification, inspect per-class changes and examples near decision boundaries; a low average absolute difference can still hide an important decision flip.

Here is a small summarizer for arrays collected by a benchmark harness. It assumes both latency arrays contain milliseconds and each output array corresponds to the same input order, with one row per request and one column per model output:

import numpy as np


def latency_summary(samples_ms):
    values = np.asarray(samples_ms, dtype=np.float64)
    return {
        "p50_ms": float(np.percentile(values, 50)),
        "p95_ms": float(np.percentile(values, 95)),
        "p99_ms": float(np.percentile(values, 99)),
    }


def parity_summary(outputs_fp32, outputs_int8):
    fp32 = np.asarray(outputs_fp32, dtype=np.float64)
    int8 = np.asarray(outputs_int8, dtype=np.float64)
    per_request_delta = np.mean(np.abs(fp32 - int8), axis=-1)
    return {
        "mean_absolute_delta": float(np.mean(per_request_delta)),
        "p95_absolute_delta": float(np.percentile(per_request_delta, 95)),
    }

These summaries do not replace task-specific evaluation. For example, also record whether top-class predictions or other decision thresholds changed.

Control and record variance

Use the same machine and runtime configuration for each comparison. Note background load, CPU power state, affinity or isolation settings if you use them, and any other workload sharing the device. Repeat runs and compare run-to-run variation. If the host cannot be isolated, state that plainly.

Use a representative validation set for accuracy and parity. Synthetic inputs are valuable for exercising a harness or pipeline, but they cannot establish how a model behaves on the real input distribution.

Keep calibration and benchmark series distinct

Calibration data influences the quantization parameters. Record its source and important characteristics, and keep the evaluation set separate. If calibration changes, treat the quantized model as a new artifact and rerun the full comparison rather than blending results from different model versions.

Make precision and execution path observable

If some requests fall back from INT8 to FP32, label them. Do not combine them into one “INT8” result. Emit structured output—JSON works well—with model hashes, precision, device, warm-up configuration, sample count, latency distribution, output deltas, and run metadata.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • Simple harness vs. realistic load: a single-request loop is easy to understand, but it does not characterize concurrency or resource contention.
  • Synthetic inputs vs. representative data: synthetic inputs make a repeatable demo; production claims need appropriate evaluation inputs.
  • Tail reporting vs. small samples: percentiles reveal latency spread, but only when there are enough measurements to support them.
  • Mixed precision vs. clean comparison: unreported fallbacks make speed and parity comparisons untrustworthy.

Try it yourself

  1. Write down whether you are testing cold start, latency, throughput, or a combination.
  2. Warm up deliberately and record the sample count and test conditions.
  3. Report FP32 and INT8 percentiles alongside output-delta and decision-change summaries.
  4. Repeat on an idle host and under representative load; keep those results separate.

Closing thought

Benchmarking honestly is a habit. Warm up, report the distribution, compare outputs, and describe the machine and workload. Then “it’s faster” becomes a claim another engineer can reproduce and assess.

Further reading

  • OpenVINO throughput benchmark sample
  • OpenVINO performance measurement FAQ
  • OpenVINO inference optimization guidance

atom:entry.atom:title: Contribution Guidelines Nobody Reads: Designing Onboarding That Actually Works
atom:entry.atom:summary: Most CONTRIBUTING.md files fail. Build contributor paths that get to a working PR: quickstart scripts, test-first templates, guardrails, and realistic expectations.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I maintain a small open-source project in my spare time. That means I care about contributor experience, but I don’t have limitless hours to hand-hold. The first hard lesson I learned is that most CONTRIBUTING.md files are performative: polite, informative, and easy to ignore. A good contribution guide should be a conveyor belt — once someone steps on, the belt carries them through setup, a small code change, a test run, and a PR.

A small open-source project may be maintained with limited time, so contributor experience matters. A tested quickstart, a narrow first change, and clear expectations make it easier for someone to turn an idea into a useful pull request.

The failure mode

A new contributor lands on your repo, reads a long CONTRIBUTING.md, and tries to set up the environment. They get halfway through a failing install, lose an hour chasing Python versions, and give up. Their idea never materializes, and you lose a potential collaborator. The contributions that do arrive are sporadic and often misaligned with your project norms.

What I learned

A “quickstart” that is truly quick

The first section of CONTRIBUTING.md should be a script that succeeds on a fresh machine in under 10 minutes. No optional flourishes; no “you can also…” — one path, tested regularly. In a Python project, that means creating an isolated environment, installing exact dependencies, running tests, and starting the server. If you support multiple OSes, state the best-supported environment up front and link alternatives after the main path.

Example quickstart

# clone + setup
git clone https://github.com/yourname/your-project && cd your-project
python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt
# run tests
pytest -q
# start service
uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

A first PR path that doesn’t require knowing the whole codebase

If your project supports plugins, design the first contribution as “add a simple plugin” — a single file with a single function, plus a minimal test. Scaffold the directory structure in the quickstart and provide a template file with TODOs. Make it obvious what a valid plugin looks like and how it integrates.

Minimal plugin template

# your_project/plugins/example_plugin.py
from your_project.core import EvidenceSource, EvidenceResult
class ExamplePlugin(EvidenceSource):
    name = "example_plugin"
def evaluate(self, profile: dict) -> EvidenceResult:
    # TODO: basic rule: if profile has 'example' flag, return a small boost
if profile.get("example", False):
    return EvidenceResult.present(score_delta=0.05, note="example flag")
    return EvidenceResult.missing(reason="no example flag")

Tests are not optional — make them the easiest path

Require a test in your PR template, but help contributors succeed by including a ready-made test template that imports the plugin and checks a tiny scenario. Fewer than 20 lines is perfect, and the test should run fast.

PR checklist and matching test

### Checklist
- [ ] Added a test covering the plugin behavior
- [ ] Ran `pytest -q` locally
- [ ] Updated plugin docs (one paragraph + example)
Test template:
# tests/test_example_plugin.py
from your_project.plugins.example_plugin import ExamplePlugin
from your_project.core import EvidenceResult
def test_example_plugin_with_flag():
plugin = ExamplePlugin()
result = plugin.evaluate({"example": True})
assert isinstance(result, EvidenceResult)
assert result.type == "present"
assert result.note == "example flag"

Labeling matters more than exhortations

A “good first issue” label is a real signal. Curate it weekly: choose small, well-bounded tasks with a single file change and a single test. Avoid issues that depend on strategic decisions or require deep context. If you don’t have time to curate, do fewer but better — five solid good-first-issues beat twenty vague ones.

“How to ask for help” — define the format, not the channel

New contributors often ask for help with missing context. Provide a brief template for help requests: environment, exact command, full error output, and what they already tried. Keep it short and clear. This reduces back-and-forth and helps you respond faster.

- OS and Python version:
- Exact command:
- Full error output (paste as a code block):
- What I’ve tried so far:

The social contract: response-time expectations

State expected response windows for maintainers. If you maintain the project in spare time, say so. Set realistic targets for issue triage and pull request reviews, then keep them visible. Set expectations, and you’ll reduce anxiety on both sides.

CI that reduces guesswork

Your CI should run tests and sanity checks on every PR with clear messages. If a plugin interface requires a test, fail with a helpful note when none is detected. If the project uses a formatting or linting standard, automate the fix script and link it from the failure output.

Trade-offs and failure modes

Trade-offs

Prescriptive quickstart vs flexibility: You’ll help more contributors by picking one supported path; you’ll disappoint a few who prefer different tools. Document alternatives briefly but keep the main path simple.

Template rigor vs contributor creativity: Templates guide good behavior but can feel constraining. Invite advanced contributions after the first PR; keep the first path narrow and friendly.

CI strictness vs PR throughput: Strict checks reduce maintainers’ manual work but increase initial friction. Counterbalance with crystal-clear failure messages and one-line fix commands.

Failure modes

“Wall of text”: Long CONTRIBUTING.md that reads more like a policy than a path. Solution: front-load the quickstart and the first PR template; move policies to the bottom.

“Passes locally, fails in CI”: Version and environment differences. Solution: pin dependencies, provide a lock or requirements file, and document the supported Python version.

“Invisible expectations”: Unstated response windows or required tests. Solution: PR templates and CI checks that make expectations explicit.

Try it yourself

Rewrite the top of your CONTRIBUTING.md into a tested quickstart that succeeds in under 10 minutes.

Add a one-file plugin template and a matching test template. Wire CI to require a test for new plugins.

Curate five “good first issue” tickets with single-file changes and clear acceptance criteria. Measure issue and review response times, then adjust your maintainer schedule accordingly.

Further reading

  • GitHub Docs: Issue and pull request templates
  • GitHub Docs: Community health files

atom:entry.atom:title: Practical secrets with OCI Vault: creation, rotation, and usage
atom:entry.atom:summary: Storing application credentials in Vault and rotating them without writing custom scripts everywhere.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A database password in an environment variable or a config file is a leak waiting for a screenshot, a log line or a copied image. The harder question is operational: who creates the secret, how does the app read it, and what happens when it changes?

I wanted one flow that answers all three, so rotation is a normal event instead of a project.

Options and trade-offs

  • Secrets in files or environment variables: fast to start, and prone to leaks and drift.
  • A non-OCI secret store: a good option if you already run one, with extra integration and policy work.
  • OCI Vault secrets: IAM-governed, versioned, with rotation options. It needs deliberate policies and a read path.

My recommendation

Create the secret in a vault, with a master encryption key in the same vault, and let the application read the current version at runtime using an instance or resource principal. Rotate sensitive credentials on a schedule and watch the audit log for reads.

Worked example

Reading a secret from Java with an instance principal. Secret content comes back base64 encoded, so decode it and keep it in memory.

var provider = InstancePrincipalsAuthenticationDetailsProvider.builder().build();
try (var secrets = SecretsClient.builder().build(provider)) {
    var req = GetSecretBundleRequest.builder()
            .secretId(System.getenv("DB_SECRET_OCID"))
            .stage(GetSecretBundleRequest.Stage.Current)
            .build();
    var content = (Base64SecretBundleContentDetails)
            secrets.getSecretBundle(req).getSecretBundle().getSecretBundleContent();
    byte[] password = java.util.Base64.getDecoder().decode(content.getContent());
    // use the bytes, then discard them; do not log them
}

The policy that lets only the runtime read that one secret:

Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to read secret-bundles in compartment apps
  where target.secret.id = '<db_secret_ocid>'

Rotation can be configured on the secret with an interval, or driven through a function that updates the target system, such as an Autonomous Database user, and then writes a new secret version. Because every version has a stage such as current or previous, you can roll back by pointing readers at the earlier version while you investigate.

Checklist

  1. Create the secret with a key in the same vault.
  2. Authorize only the runtime principal to read secret bundles.
  3. Decode at runtime, hold the value in memory and never log it.
  4. Turn on rotation for credentials that matter.
  5. Alert on unusual GetSecretBundle activity in the audit log.
  6. Write down how to restore the previous version if a rotation fails.

Where this doesn't apply

One-time tokens that never need to be read again do not need a vault entry. Very large blobs may also exceed the secret size limit, so check the current limit before choosing Vault for them.

One honest limitation

Rotation and cross-region replication add moving parts. I rehearse a rotation in a test environment before the first production run.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Vault, Creating a Secret
  • OCI Documentation: Updating a Secret and Secret Rotation
  • OCI Documentation: Retrieving a Secret Bundle (Java SDK)

atom:entry.atom:title: Smaller, Quieter, Safer: A Production Image Checklist
atom:entry.atom:summary: A practical production Docker image checklist covering multi-stage builds, non-root users, build context, secrets, and health checks.
atom:entry.atom:content:
A production container should be small enough to move efficiently, quiet enough to operate, and constrained enough to limit avoidable risk. Those outcomes come from simple habits: keep build tools out of the runtime image, use a non-root identity, keep the build context tight, and make health checks cheap.

The aceu-trust-demo uses a multi-stage build, a slim base, a non-root user, a health endpoint, and Compose for local runs. The checklist below is designed to make those decisions repeatable.

1. Keep build tools out of the runtime stage

Compilers, headers, and test tools belong in a build stage when the running application does not need them. Copy only the installed runtime dependencies and application code into the final stage. A smaller image can reduce transfer time and remove packages the service does not need.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
RUN python -m venv /venv
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH"
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY aceu ./aceu

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --create-home appuser
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /venv /venv
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /app/aceu ./aceu
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH" \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen("http://localhost:8000/health", timeout=2)' || exit 1
CMD ["uvicorn", "aceu.app:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Check the actual base image and application requirements before using this verbatim. For example, a health endpoint must exist and return a failing status when the process is unhealthy.

2. Choose a base image for the runtime

A minimal base can reduce unnecessary packages, but it may omit a system library your app needs. Add required runtime packages explicitly, then measure the result. Pick an image the team can patch and operate; “smallest possible” is not the only goal.

3. Run as a non-root user with a known UID

Use an explicit user ID and make sure files copied into the image are readable by that user. If a writeable directory is needed, grant access only to that path. Fix ownership in the Dockerfile instead of switching back to root when a permissions error appears.

4. Keep the build context narrow

Docker can only build from the context it receives. Exclude local caches, virtual environments, repository history, and secrets with a .dockerignore file:

__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
.env
.git/
node_modules/
venv/
.venv/
dist/
build/

Review COPY statements as carefully as ignore rules. Do not copy test fixtures or private configuration into the runtime image unless the application needs them.

5. Keep secrets out of image layers

Do not place credentials in Dockerfile ARG or ENV instructions, and do not copy secret files into a layer. Prefer platform-managed runtime secrets. When a build genuinely needs a secret, use BuildKit’s secret mount rather than baking it into the image.

6. Check for weakened isolation and noisy health checks

Review Dockerfiles and deployment manifests for settings that weaken isolation, such as an unconfined seccomp profile. Keep health checks bounded and inexpensive; an overly aggressive check can add load or mark a service unhealthy during a temporary resource spike. Set log levels intentionally so normal operation does not bury useful signals.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • Slim image vs. hidden dependencies: add the libraries you need, then verify the runtime stage starts and serves its critical paths.
  • Non-root vs. file permissions: set ownership during build and grant write access only where needed.
  • Health checks vs. extra load: probe a fast path and use a reasonable timeout and interval.
  • Runtime secrets vs. rotation work: secure injection adds operational responsibilities, so document ownership and rotation clearly.

Common surprises include a credential accidentally left in an image layer, a slim runtime missing a required shared library, or a non-root process unable to read a root-owned file. A deliberate image review catches these before deployment.

Try it on your next image

  1. Separate build and runtime stages, then compare the resulting image size.
  2. Run the application under a non-root UID and verify file access.
  3. Add a .dockerignore file and inspect the build context.
  4. Add a CI lint step for known unsafe Dockerfile or manifest settings.

Closing thought

A smaller, quieter, safer image is easier to move and less likely to surprise the team in production. The demo remains illustrative; the container practices are the reusable part.

Further reading

  • Docker build best practices
  • Docker multi-stage builds
  • Build secrets with Docker

atom:entry.atom:title: The Conversion Gap: From ONNX Export to an Optimized Runtime Format
atom:entry.atom:summary: A practical path from ONNX to OpenVINO IR: inspect operators, handle conversion gaps, and validate output parity.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Training and production are different environments. Exporting a model to ONNX is a useful boundary, but a production runtime still needs to understand the graph, shapes, operators, and precision choices. Conversion friction is easier to handle when it is planned for instead of discovered at release time.

In aceu-edge-infer, I convert a lightweight classifier from ONNX for use with OpenVINO. One custom activation exposed an operator gap and required a conservative CPU fallback. The demo’s ACE-U output is illustrative, not an evaluation of real people; the model-delivery practices here are the focus.

Check the graph before you convert

Inspect the ONNX graph, its opset, input names, and shapes. Look for custom operators and operations that may not be supported by the runtime version or target device. If the model has dynamic dimensions, decide which shapes production must support and test those explicitly.

OpenVINO can convert supported ONNX models to IR, and it can also read ONNX directly at runtime. Conversion is useful when you want a prepared artifact and predictable model-load behavior; first confirm the format is supported and that conversion solves a real deployment need.

Use the current conversion API

For a supported ONNX model, the OpenVINO Python API can convert and save an IR artifact:

import openvino as ov
from pathlib import Path

model = ov.convert_model("models/classifier.onnx")
output = Path("build/ir_fp32/classifier.xml")
output.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
ov.save_model(model, output)

The saved IR consists of an XML graph and a weights file. Alternatively, the ovc command-line tool can convert supported input models. Keep the exact command or script, OpenVINO version, input shapes, and conversion logs with the build so another engineer can reproduce it.

Read conversion errors as signals

  • Unsupported or partially supported operators: check the runtime’s supported operations and determine whether a supported equivalent preserves behavior.
  • Shape inference failures: inspect dynamic dimensions and provide explicit input shapes only when they match the model’s intended use.
  • Precision-specific differences: validate the FP32 conversion first; quantization adds a separate source of numerical change.
  • Custom layers: decide early whether to replace, isolate, or route around the operation.

Choose a fallback deliberately

If an operator cannot use the preferred execution path, there are several options:

  • Replace it with a supported equivalent, then measure output parity and confirm the change fits the model’s accuracy budget.
  • Keep a documented CPU implementation for the unsupported portion when the runtime and architecture support that boundary.
  • Split a larger graph into a supported model and a small, explicit post-processing step in application code.

Do not label a fallback as “optimized” without measurement. Surface the selected runtime path in logs or response metadata, and make clear whether the service can continue safely when the preferred path is unavailable.

Validate outputs before optimizing precision

Create a golden evaluation set and compare the source ONNX model with the converted FP32 model first. Define acceptance criteria that fit the task—for example, maximum per-class delta or mean absolute error. If outputs differ, compare intermediate tensors where possible to locate the first divergence.

Only after conversion parity is understood should you evaluate INT8. This keeps operator-conversion differences separate from quantization differences and makes failures much easier to diagnose.

Make conversion part of the build

Script input shapes, conversion flags, substitutions, and output paths. Version IR artifacts with the model and code revision that produced them; record file hashes and conversion logs rather than overwriting a vague latest artifact. Run conversion in CI when the model, conversion script, or runtime version changes.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • Operator replacement vs. behavioral fidelity: an equivalent-looking function can change output; verify parity against the task’s acceptance criteria.
  • CPU fallback vs. uniform execution: a fallback can preserve service behavior but adds a path to test and monitor.
  • Fast manual fix vs. reproducibility: one-off flags may unblock a conversion, while a scripted fix makes future builds repeatable.

A model that converts and runs can still produce different outputs. A fallback that is not disclosed can make performance results misleading. A runtime update can change what converts successfully, so keep conversion inside the change-review process.

Try it yourself

  1. Inventory operators, opset, shapes, and custom layers in your ONNX file.
  2. Convert to IR with a scripted, versioned command and retain its logs.
  3. Compare outputs on a golden set before you introduce quantization.
  4. Document and test every fallback path, including how the service reports it.

Closing thought

The conversion gap is manageable when operator compatibility, model parity, and fallbacks are treated as product requirements. Script the path, version what it creates, and validate the outputs before optimizing further.

Further reading

  • Convert supported models to OpenVINO IR
  • Set and validate model input shapes
  • ONNX operator specifications

atom:entry.atom:title: Building multi-architecture images when your laptop is arm64 and your servers are x86
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I publish one image tag that runs on Apple Silicon and on x86 hosts, and why I avoid emulation for anything that matters.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

I develop on an arm64 laptop, and a lot of the places I deploy to are x86. If I push an image built only for my laptop, the failure shows up later and far from the cause, usually as an unhelpful exec format error on a server. Docker can build for several platforms in one command, but there are a few traps: emulation is slow and sometimes subtly wrong, vendor binaries downloaded during a build may be for the wrong CPU, and a manifest that is missing a platform fails on pull.

Options and trade-offs

  • Build only for the laptop architecture: quick, but it breaks the first time the image runs elsewhere.
  • Build every platform under emulation: one command, but slow, and it only proves the code starts, not that it behaves.
  • Build natively per architecture, or avoid per-architecture work entirely: fastest and most faithful, but it needs either runners for each architecture or a build that does not depend on the CPU.

My recommendation

Be explicit about platforms and publish a manifest list. For JVM services, I go one step further: compile the jar once on the build platform, because bytecode is architecture independent, and only the runtime image differs per platform. That removes emulation from the expensive step.

Worked example

The build stage is pinned to the platform doing the build, so it runs natively. Only the small runtime stage is produced per target architecture.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./gradlew --no-daemon installDist -x test

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
ARG TARGETARCH
WORKDIR /opt/app
COPY --from=build /src/build/install/app/ ./
RUN echo "runtime image for ${TARGETARCH}"
ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/app/bin/app"]
docker buildx create --name multiarch --use
docker buildx inspect --bootstrap

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t registry.example.com/demo/app:1.4.2 \
  --push .

docker buildx imagetools inspect registry.example.com/demo/app:1.4.2

A tiny smoke test confirms which architecture you are actually running on:

public class Arch {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(System.getProperty("os.name") + " / " + System.getProperty("os.arch"));
    }
}
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 registry.example.com/demo/app:1.4.2
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 registry.example.com/demo/app:1.4.2

Checklist

  1. State --platform explicitly, every time.
  2. Run the compile step on the build platform when the output is architecture independent.
  3. Check any downloaded binary against the target architecture.
  4. Inspect the pushed manifest list and confirm every platform you need is present.
  5. Run real tests on native hardware for each platform you ship.

Where this doesn't apply

If you ship native code (JNI libraries, native-image binaries, or CPU-specific agents), the compile step is no longer architecture independent, and you need native builds for each target.

One honest limitation

Emulation is useful for a smoke test and not much else. It can hide timing and system-call differences, and a JIT-heavy workload will behave differently from the real thing.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Multi-platform builds
  • Docker Docs: buildx imagetools inspect
  • Docker Docs: Multi-stage builds (BUILDPLATFORM and TARGETARCH)

atom:entry.atom:title: Identity Domains: MFA policies and admin-safe rollout
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I turn on MFA without locking the administrators out of their own console.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Turning on MFA is the right call, and it is also the change most likely to produce a locked-out admin at 5 p.m. on a Friday. Automation that signs in as a user can break as well.

My goal was a rollout order that protects administrators first, leaves one deliberate escape hatch while things settle, and then closes that hatch.

Options and trade-offs

  • Default MFA settings alone: simple, but they may not cover administrator-specific rules, so validate which factors are really enabled.
  • Custom sign-on policies: fine-grained control by group and application, at the cost of more configuration.
  • The pre-seeded console security policy: a good starting point aimed at administrators. It still needs testing and a plan for exceptions.

My recommendation

Enable the factors first, including a phishing-resistant one such as FIDO2 or a passkey. Then enforce through a sign-on policy with the administrator rule at the top and an all-users rule beneath it. Exempt one administrator temporarily, confirm everyone else can sign in, and remove the exemption quickly.

Worked example

The rollout order I use. Rule order matters, because sign-on rules are evaluated from the top.

1. Enable factors: FIDO2/passkey, mobile app notification/passcode.
   Generate a bypass code and store it somewhere offline.
2. Open the sign-on policy for the console (or create one).
3. Rule 1 (top):  group = Administrators  -> require MFA
   Rule 2:        all users                -> require MFA
4. Exclude ONE named admin while you test. Keep a second session open.
5. Sign in with a private browser window as an admin and as a normal user.
6. Remove the exclusion. Re-test enrollment and re-authentication.
7. Confirm service accounts and automation use API keys or a client
   application, not interactive user sign-in.

Before you flip enforcement, check that you can still reach the tenancy through a path that does not depend on the new rule, such as a confidential application that calls the REST API.

Checklist

  1. Enable phishing-resistant factors, and keep a bypass code stored offline.
  2. Put the administrator rule first, then the all-users rule.
  3. Exclude a single administrator temporarily, and remove that exclusion on a set date.
  4. Test enrollment and re-authentication in a private window.
  5. Write the support steps for a user who loses their device.
  6. Watch sign-in failures for the first few days and adjust.

Where this doesn't apply

Non-interactive automation should not go through user MFA. Give it API keys, instance principals or a client application with its own controls.

One honest limitation

Each additional factor adds friction at sign-in and at recovery. I weigh how easy it is to enroll and recover against the security gain, especially for infrequent users.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Managing Multifactor Authentication in Identity Domains
  • OCI Documentation: Managing Sign-On Policies
  • OCI Documentation: Security Policy for OCI Console

atom:entry.atom:title: Faster Isn’t Free: The Real Trade-offs of Quantizing a Model from FP32 to INT8
atom:entry.atom:summary: How to evaluate INT8 quantization honestly by measuring latency, output fidelity, calibration coverage, and production risk.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I’ve shipped CPU-only inference, and I’ve also declined to ship a “faster” model when the trade-off did not hold up. Quantizing a model from FP32 to INT8 can help meet latency or memory goals. It can also change outputs in ways that matter to the people relying on them.

In my public demo, aceu-edge-infer, I use a small ONNX classifier converted to OpenVINO IR and maintain FP32 and INT8 variants. The service reports which precision it used. It returns four ACE-U dimensions—Authenticity, Credibility, Empathy, and Uniqueness—but these are illustrative outputs from a demo, not validated judgments of real people. The engineering questions are the useful part.

Why quantization can help—and why it changes behavior

Quantization represents selected model weights and activations using lower-precision values. With fewer bits to move and process, an inference path may use less memory and run faster on compatible hardware. The actual speedup depends on the model, operators, runtime, and target device; INT8 is not a universal fast switch.

Lower precision also introduces rounding. Small changes in early layers can flow through later layers, and a score close to a decision threshold may move across it. Some operators quantize cleanly; others may need different quantization settings, to remain in higher precision, or to run through a fallback path.

Look for where the errors gather

Aggregate accuracy can hide concentrated regressions. Compare FP32 and INT8 outputs by class and by meaningful input slice. Inspect examples near decision boundaries, rare patterns, and values near the extremes of the calibration distribution. A useful audit asks not only “How much did the average score move?” but also “Where did the model change its decision?”

Calibrate on data that resembles use

Post-training quantization uses calibration samples to estimate ranges for activations. If the samples do not resemble the inputs the service will see, those ranges can be a poor fit. Include representative cases and the edge cases you care about. When real data cannot be used, diverse synthetic examples can help exercise the pipeline, but they do not replace evaluation on an appropriate held-out set.

A minimal OpenVINO/NNCF sketch looks like this. calibration_samples must yield preprocessed examples in the model’s expected input format:

import nncf
import openvino as ov

core = ov.Core()
model = core.read_model("model_fp32.xml")
calibration_dataset = nncf.Dataset(calibration_samples)

model_int8 = nncf.quantize(model, calibration_dataset)
ov.save_model(model_int8, "model_int8.xml")

This produces a quantized model; it does not establish that the model is accurate enough for a particular use. Keep calibration data and evaluation data separate, and record the evaluation results alongside the model artifact.

Measure more than a mean

  • Latency distribution: report p50, p95, and p99 for both precisions. A mean alone can hide a worse tail.
  • Output deltas: compare score changes and decision changes across the evaluation set.
  • Warm-up: exclude initialization and compilation work from steady-state measurements, but report cold-start behavior separately if it matters in production.
  • Representative conditions: use the same device, request shape, batch size, concurrency, and preprocessing path.

The demo contains a small harness that runs synthetic requests against both variants. Its results are scaffolding until measured on an appropriate workload; synthetic measurements should never be presented as production performance.

Know when not to ship INT8

If the latency improvement is marginal while the output changes affect a high-importance class, the trade-off may be negative. For sensitive applications, stability can matter more than a modest speed gain. Compare other options too: batching, request scheduling, a different CPU pool, or optimizing a costly preprocessing step may achieve the goal with less model-level change.

Make precision visible and roll out in steps

Record the precision and execution device in service logs or response metadata so a change is diagnosable. Keep the public response contract minimal and avoid exposing sensitive implementation details.

Before a full rollout, run FP32 and INT8 in shadow for a representative sample and alert on meaningful divergence. If one slice regresses, route it back to FP32 or disable the INT8 path while you investigate. Maintaining both variants adds operational work, but gives the team a controlled recovery option.

Try it yourself

  1. Build FP32 and INT8 variants and disclose the precision used for each request.
  2. Measure warm and cold paths separately, then report latency percentiles and output-delta distributions.
  3. Evaluate by class and edge-case slice, not only by aggregate accuracy.
  4. Run a shadow comparison and define in advance what divergence will trigger a rollback.

Closing thought

Quantization is powerful, but faster is not free. Percentiles, output deltas, and slice-level evaluation tell you whether INT8 belongs in the production path—or whether FP32 is the more responsible choice.

Further reading

  • OpenVINO post-training quantization overview
  • NNCF basic quantization flow and calibration datasets
  • OpenVINO CPU device and supported inference precisions

atom:entry.atom:title: Same Dockerfile, Different Build: Reproducible Container Builds
atom:entry.atom:summary: Pin dependencies, use lock files, and verify container artifacts to make local and cloud builds more reproducible.
atom:entry.atom:content:
I once pushed a change after a healthy local run of aceu-trust-demo. The cloud build resolved a newer FastAPI version—0.142.2 instead of 0.141.1 locally—and pulled an additional package, opentelemetry-api. The Dockerfile was the same; the dependency ranges were not locked.

That kind of drift is easy to miss. A repeatable build takes more than a Dockerfile: it needs a locked dependency graph, a deliberate base-image update policy, and a way to inspect the artifact that actually shipped.

Why “same Dockerfile” can produce a different image

Version ranges allow resolvers to choose newer compatible releases. A mutable base-image tag can also point to a newer image later. Build caches may keep an older layer locally while CI fetches fresh inputs. The source recipe is unchanged, but the resolved inputs differ.

Lock the dependency graph

Use exact direct-dependency pins and commit a lock file that records the resolved transitive versions. Where the package manager supports it, include hashes and install in locked mode. A short input file might look like this:

# requirements.in — human-maintained direct dependencies
fastapi==0.141.1
uvicorn==0.30.1

# Resolve and lock transitive dependencies, including hashes.
pip-compile --generate-hashes --output-file requirements.txt requirements.in

Commit both files. Install from the generated lock in CI rather than re-resolving ranges during every image build:

pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt

Pins make change deliberate; they do not remove the need to update packages for fixes.

Choose tags or digests deliberately

Tags are convenient and can move to newer images. Digests identify a specific image immutably. A digest gives a reproducible base, but it will not advance to security fixes on its own—you must monitor updates and refresh it deliberately.

# Illustrative digest placeholder: replace with a verified digest
FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:<verified-digest>

If you use tags, track when they change and refresh the base during scheduled builds. --pull tells Docker to attempt to pull referenced images before the build:

docker build --pull --tag aceu-trust-demo:main .

Make updates reviewable

Use a dependency update bot or scheduled update pull requests, then gate those changes with tests and image scanning. For production-critical dependencies, document which updates need an explicit reviewer. Prefer a visible, tested update over a silent change arriving through a floating version range.

Keep registry access safe and documented

CI needs a clear path to authenticate, tag, and push. Store credentials in the CI secret manager, use a short-lived token where available, and send passwords over standard input instead of exposing them in command arguments:

# REGISTRY_USER and REGISTRY_TOKEN come from the CI secret store.
printf '%s' "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | docker login "$REGISTRY_HOST" \
  --username "$REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin

IMAGE="$REGISTRY_HOST/aceu-trust-demo:$GIT_SHA"
docker build --pull --tag "$IMAGE" .
docker push "$IMAGE"

Document who owns the credentials, how rotation works, and what a failed login looks like. Never print secret values into build logs.

Compare artifacts when behavior changes

If local and cloud behavior diverge, inspect the image’s package inventory or generate an SBOM. Compare the resolved versions and base-image digest, then decide whether to re-lock, refresh the image, or accept the change with an appropriate test update. Looking at the built artifact beats guessing from the Dockerfile alone.

Trade-offs and failure modes

  • Exact pins vs. security updates: pins improve repeatability, while scheduled updates and scans keep them current.
  • Tags vs. digests: tags are easier to refresh; digests make the selected base explicit and immutable.
  • Locks vs. setup time: generating a lock adds a step, but saves time when builds need to be compared.
  • Registry authentication: expired tokens or changed scopes should produce an explicit CI failure, not a misleading successful pipeline.

Try it in your pipeline

  1. Replace floating version ranges with exact direct pins and commit a full lock file.
  2. Pick a base-image policy: tag plus scheduled refresh, or digest plus an explicit update cadence.
  3. Build with --pull when you want CI to check for updated base images.
  4. Record the image tag or digest produced by CI and inspect its packages when behavior changes.

Closing thought

“Same Dockerfile” rarely guarantees “same runtime.” Lock files, explicit base-image policy, and artifact inspection turn hidden drift into a change the team can review.

Further reading

  • Docker Buildx build options, including --pull and SBOM attestations
  • Pulling an image by immutable digest
  • pip-tools documentation for Python dependency locking

atom:entry.atom:title: Identity Domains: SAML/OIDC federation setup notes
atom:entry.atom:summary: What I configure first so an external identity provider works cleanly with OCI.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Most teams already have an identity provider such as Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) or Okta, and nobody wants a second set of passwords for the cloud console. Federation solves that, but a careless setup can lock out administrators or leave group membership drifting away from what the IdP says.

I wanted a repeatable order of operations that keeps a way back in at every step.

Options and trade-offs

  • Console setup: straightforward and visible, and it needs careful mapping and testing.
  • API or automation: repeatable, but there are more moving parts to get wrong the first time.
  • Default sign-on and IdP policies versus custom rules: the defaults are a fine start, but confirm what they do to administrators before you rely on them.

My recommendation

Use the Identity Domains flow with a SAML identity provider. Exchange metadata, decide which assertion attribute identifies the user, map IdP groups to IAM groups, and test with a staged non-admin account before an administrator. Change federation and MFA separately so a problem can be traced to one change.

Worked example

The sequence I follow in the Console. It is a checklist, not a script, because the exact screens differ a little between tenancies.

1. Keep a local break-glass admin that does NOT use the new IdP.
2. Identity Domains > Security > Identity providers > Add SAML IdP.
   - Upload the IdP metadata XML (or enter the endpoints and signing cert).
   - Choose the attribute that carries the username (NameID or email).
3. Export the domain's service provider metadata and import it into the IdP.
4. Map IdP groups to IAM groups (group mapping / JIT provisioning).
5. Add the IdP to an identity provider policy rule and activate it.
6. Test: non-admin user first, then an admin. Confirm group-based access.
7. Record the metadata expiry date and who owns the mapping table.

For Entra ID the pattern is the same. You create an enterprise application, upload the service provider metadata, download the federation metadata XML and import it into the domain. OIDC-based identity providers follow the same ideas, with a client ID and secret in place of metadata files.

Checklist

  1. Keep a break-glass local administrator outside federation.
  2. Document the group mappings and name an owner for each.
  3. Test a non-admin sign-in before you test an admin sign-in.
  4. Watch for attribute mismatches, and fix the mapping instead of widening a policy.
  5. Track the IdP signing certificate expiry and the metadata refresh process.
  6. Do not change federation and MFA policy in the same maintenance window.

Where this doesn't apply

A very small tenancy with no external IdP is better off with local users and a strong sign-on policy. Federation adds value when there is already an identity source to follow.

One honest limitation

An expired or rotated IdP certificate can break sign-in without warning. I keep a calendar entry for it and a short, written refresh procedure.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Federating with Identity Domains (SAML identity providers)
  • OCI Documentation: Identity Provider Policies in Identity Domains
  • OCI Documentation: Manually Federating Your Tenancy

atom:entry.atom:title: Faster Docker builds for a Java service: context, layers and cache mounts
atom:entry.atom:summary: Most of the speed-up comes from three boring changes: a smaller build context, a sensible layer order and a BuildKit cache mount for Gradle.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

When a container build takes minutes, people stop iterating and start batching changes, which is when bugs hide. Teams usually respond by turning caching on and hoping. That helps a little, but the real gains come from what you send to the builder and the order you ask it to do things in. A Java service is a good case. The dependencies change rarely and the source changes constantly, yet a naive Dockerfile downloads the world on every edit.

Options and trade-offs

  • Do nothing and rely on the default layer cache: fine until the first COPY of the whole repo, after which every code change re-downloads dependencies.
  • Copy only the build files first, resolve dependencies, then copy the source: much better, but a changed build file still re-downloads everything.
  • Add a BuildKit cache mount for the Gradle home: dependency downloads survive across builds, even when the layer itself is invalidated.

My recommendation

Start with a .dockerignore, because it is the cheapest win. Order layers from least to most volatile, use a cache mount for the dependency cache, and use a multi-stage build so the JDK and build tools stay out of the runtime image. Pin dependency versions so speed does not come at the cost of repeatability.

Worked example

A two-stage Dockerfile for a Gradle project. The cache mount is only available during the RUN step, so the build that needs it happens inside the same step.

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src

# Build files first: this layer only changes when dependencies change
COPY gradlew settings.gradle.kts build.gradle.kts ./
COPY gradle gradle
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.gradle \
    ./gradlew --no-daemon dependencies > /dev/null

# Source last: this is the layer that changes on every edit
COPY src src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.gradle \
    ./gradlew --no-daemon installDist -x test

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /opt/app
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --create-home appuser
COPY --from=build /src/build/install/app/ ./
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/app/bin/app"]

And the context file that keeps the build fast before any layer is considered:

.git
.gradle/
build/
out/
*.iml
.idea/
.env

To see the effect, time a cold build, change one line of source, and time it again:

time DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -t demo/app:dev .
echo '// touch' >> src/main/java/App.java
time docker build -t demo/app:dev .

The second build should skip the dependency steps entirely. Bump a dependency version and confirm that step does re-run.

Checklist

  1. Add a .dockerignore before changing anything else.
  2. Copy build files, resolve dependencies, then copy source.
  3. Use a cache mount for the Gradle home, and run the build in the same RUN step.
  4. Use a multi-stage build and run as a non-root user.
  5. Pin dependency versions, and rebuild without cache now and then to catch drift.

Where this doesn't apply

If your dependencies change on every commit, or the project is tiny, none of this will be noticeable. A remote build service with its own cache may also change which of these steps matter.

One honest limitation

Cache mounts live on the builder, not in the image, so a fresh CI runner starts cold unless you export and import the cache. A fast local build says little about a CI build.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Optimize cache usage in builds
  • Docker Docs: Multi-stage builds
  • Docker Docs: Dockerfile reference (RUN --mount)
  • Docker Docs: .dockerignore

atom:entry.atom:title: Dynamic groups with tag-based scoping (illustrative patterns)
atom:entry.atom:summary: Using compartment and tag rules so only the instances you intend can assume a group's permissions.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

A dynamic group rule that says "every instance in compartment X" is easy to write and easy to regret. The day someone launches a test box or a bastion in that compartment, it silently picks up the same permissions as your production services.

I wanted membership that is predictable and explainable: this instance is in the group because it is in this compartment and carries this tag.

Options and trade-offs

  • Compartment-only rules: simple, with broad membership that grows by accident.
  • Instance OCID rules: exact, but you edit the rule every time an instance is replaced.
  • Compartment plus tag rules: precise enough for most teams, as long as tagging is governed.

My recommendation

I combine a compartment OCID with a defined tag namespace, key and value, joined with ALL so both conditions must be true. Then I treat the tag like an access-control input and restrict who can apply it. Without that last step, anyone who can tag an instance can effectively add it to the group.

Worked example

A rule that requires both the compartment and the tag. The tag here uses a namespace called department and a key called runtime.

ALL {instance.compartment.id = '<apps_compartment_ocid>',
     tag.department.runtime.value = 'payments'}

When a group should cover two compartments, use ANY around the compartment checks and keep the tag condition outside it:

ALL {
  ANY {instance.compartment.id = '<apps_compartment_ocid>',
       instance.compartment.id = '<shared_compartment_ocid>'},
  tag.department.runtime.value = 'payments'
}

The Console rule builder covers the simple cases, but you will type tag rules by hand. Changes to a rule or to a tag are not instant, so I verify the effective membership rather than assuming it, and I keep the rule text in version control next to the policy it supports.

Checklist

  1. Define the tag namespace, key and allowed values before writing the rule.
  2. Use ALL so the compartment and the tag must both match.
  3. Limit who may apply or change the tag through IAM.
  4. Keep the rule text and the reason for it in version control.
  5. Plan for a delay after rule or tag changes, and verify membership before cutting over.
  6. Re-check the effective membership after each deployment.

Where this doesn't apply

Short-lived experiments are better served by an instance-specific rule, or by a throwaway compartment that will be deleted. A tagging scheme is overhead you do not need there.

One honest limitation

The delay before membership changes take effect can surprise a rollout. I stage the change, test that the policy works for the new instances, and only then retire the old rule.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Managing Dynamic Groups (matching rules)
  • OCI Documentation: Tagging Overview
  • OCI Documentation: Calling Services from an Instance

atom:entry.atom:title: Least-privilege IAM policies for workloads (compartment-first)
atom:entry.atom:summary: The policy patterns I reach for to keep OCI access narrow, readable and easy to audit.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

IAM policies tend to grow the same way: someone is blocked, someone writes a broad statement to unblock them, and that statement lives forever. Tenancy-wide grants and "manage all-resources" lines are the usual result, and they are hard to walk back once other things depend on them.

I wanted a default that is easy to follow under time pressure. Scope every statement to a compartment, name the resource family, and pick the verb that matches the job.

Options and trade-offs

  • Tenancy-level policies: quick to write and a large blast radius. I keep them for a few shared administrative duties with tightly limited verbs.
  • Compartment-first policies: they line up with ownership and cost boundaries. The price is that you need a compartment structure and consistent names.
  • Conditional policies: precise, using where clauses on bucket, secret or operation. They also need documentation and testing, or they turn into puzzles.

My recommendation

Start in the compartment that owns the workload. OCI's verbs run from inspect to read to use to manage, so give runtime principals read or use and keep manage for operators. Prefer resource families such as instance-family or object-family over all-resources, and review the policy set on a schedule so it does not drift.

Worked example

Here is the shape I aim for with an application compartment called apps. Runtime access is narrow, and the platform team gets a separate, more powerful statement.

# Runtime: what the app itself needs
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to read objects in compartment apps
  where target.bucket.name = 'app-config'
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to use log-content in compartment apps
 
# Operators: separate group, separate statements
Allow group platform-admins to manage instance-family in compartment apps
Allow group platform-admins to read policies in compartment apps

Compare that with what usually shows up in a review:

Allow group developers to manage all-resources in tenancy

The second line is shorter and works on day one, which is why it keeps appearing. It is also impossible to explain to an auditor. When delegating to a sub-team, use a compartment path such as A:B so the grant follows the hierarchy.

Be careful with the ability to manage policies. Whoever can manage policies in a compartment can usually grant themselves more, so I keep that permission with a very small group.

Checklist

  1. Use read or use for runtime principals, and keep manage for people who operate the service.
  2. Scope by compartment, and by compartment path when delegating.
  3. Write one purpose per statement, and add a short comment on who, what and why.
  4. Use resource families instead of all-resources.
  5. Put a condition on the statements that touch sensitive buckets or secrets.
  6. Review grants on a schedule and remove the stale ones.

Where this doesn't apply

Incident response across many compartments is a case where a temporary tenancy-level grant is sensible. Time-box it, write down who approved it, and delete it when the incident closes.

One honest limitation

Narrow policies mean more statements, and more statements need maintenance. A naming convention and a template for new compartments, set up early, keep that from becoming the bottleneck.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Policy Syntax
  • OCI Documentation: Policy Reference (verbs and resource families)
  • OCI Documentation: Managing Compartments

atom:entry.atom:title: Running Is Not Ready: Operating Containerized Services
atom:entry.atom:summary: Separate startup, readiness, and liveness signals to make container rollouts safer and easier to recover.
atom:entry.atom:content:
One of the most reliable lessons from operating containerized services is simple: running is not ready. A process can be alive, a port can be open, and yet the service may not be able to handle real traffic. Treat startup, readiness, and liveness as separate concerns, verify each one deliberately, and design rollouts with recovery in mind.

This article uses a small public demo, aceu-trust-demo, as a running example. It uses a multi-stage image, a non-root user, a health endpoint, and a container deployment behind external HTTPS ingress. Its ACE-U output is illustrative and based on synthetic evidence; it is not a validated assessment of real people. The operational lessons apply more broadly.

The “green” deployment that still fails

A deployment reports “running” and the dashboard looks healthy, but requests time out. A dependency is still warming up. The process is alive, so the liveness signal stays green; the service is simply not ready to serve traffic yet. The failure began when one signal was expected to answer two different questions.

Give each signal one job

Startup: has initialization finished?

Startup covers work such as loading configuration, opening required connections, or priming a cache. Slow startup should not be mistaken for a dead process.

Readiness: can this instance take traffic now?

Readiness is a promise to callers. Keep it false until the dependencies required for the service’s critical path are available. A TCP connection alone may not be enough if the application depends on a loaded index or credentials.

Liveness: is the process stuck in a state that needs a restart?

Liveness should detect an unrecoverable condition, such as a deadlock. It should not fail merely because a downstream system is briefly unavailable: repeatedly restarting healthy processes can amplify an outage.

Docker’s HEALTHCHECK records a container health state. It does not, by itself, define how a particular load balancer or orchestrator routes traffic. In Kubernetes, configure startup, readiness, and liveness probes for their distinct purposes.

A bounded Docker health check

If Python is already part of the runtime image, a tiny local endpoint check avoids adding a separate curl package just for health status:

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c 'import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen("http://localhost:8000/health", timeout=2)' || exit 1

Keep this endpoint cheap and local. Put stricter dependency checks in a separate readiness endpoint, then configure your platform to use that endpoint to gate traffic.

Roll out in stages and predefine rollback

Do not move all traffic at once. Start with a small cohort, hold it under real load for a defined soak period, then expand. Write the rollback condition before the release—for example, a measured latency threshold sustained for a defined duration, or an error rate that crosses a set limit. The thresholds should come from the service’s baseline and risk profile, not be guessed after the rollout starts.

Shut down gracefully

When a platform scales down an idle container, the process may receive SIGTERM. Stop accepting new work, let in-flight requests finish within a deadline, close outbound clients, flush metrics, and exit. Treat SIGKILL as the forced fallback. Without a drain period, a routine scale-down can become partial writes, dangling sessions, or noisy retries.

Make the dependency chain visible

Under pressure, teams often blame the topmost service. Keep a runbook that follows dependencies below the application: runtime, network, storage, cache or index, and external services. Document how each layer fails and how to check it without adding load. Infrastructure problems such as CPU starvation, memory pressure, or network saturation can surface as application timeouts and backpressure.

A green health endpoint can also miss a heavy or rarely used path. Pair alerts with lightweight, non-sensitive transition logs such as ready=false reason=index_warming and ready=true checks=passed. A weekly on-call handoff—what broke, the likely cause, and which mitigation helped—turns recurring cold starts and slow dependency warm-ups into work the team can fix.

Trade-offs to make explicit

  • Strict readiness vs. first-green speed: better gating can delay traffic, while reducing user-facing failures.
  • Longer soak vs. delivery pace: more observation lowers rollout risk but delays full exposure.
  • Graceful drain vs. implementation effort: draining takes work; skipping it risks incomplete operations.
  • Frequent liveness checks vs. flapping: overly sensitive checks can restart a service during resource spikes and worsen an incident.

Try it in your service

  1. Add a separate /ready endpoint that checks the critical dependency before returning success.
  2. Write down a staged rollout, soak period, and rollback trigger before your next release.
  3. Handle SIGTERM by draining requests and closing resources cleanly.
  4. Extend your runbook with infrastructure checks and first suspects for latency spikes.

Closing thought

Separating startup, readiness, and liveness reduces confusion during incidents and helps limit their blast radius. The demo illustrates the distinction with a local health endpoint and a reversible deployment path. Its ACE-U dimensions—Authenticity, Credibility, Empathy, and Uniqueness—remain conceptual in this context, not a judgment of real people.

Further reading

  • Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK reference
  • Kubernetes startup, readiness, and liveness probes

atom:entry.atom:title: Starting a local data pipeline in the right order, on a laptop that stays usable
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I use Compose profiles, health-gated startup and hard resource caps so a multi-service stack boots predictably and does not eat my machine.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Everyone has had the local stack that mostly works. The database is still initialising when the API connects, a worker grabs a port something else expected, and a few minutes later the fans are screaming because three containers decided they own every core. None of this is exotic. It comes from three habits: relying on start order instead of readiness, letting ports be whatever they turn out to be, and leaving resource limits at their defaults. All three are cheap to fix in a Compose file.

Options and trade-offs

  • Fixed sleeps in an entrypoint: easy to write, wrong on a slow day and wasteful on a fast one.
  • Wait-for scripts: they work, but you maintain a script per dependency and each one hides a different definition of ready.
  • Healthchecks plus depends_on with condition service_healthy: Compose does the waiting, and readiness is defined once, next to the service it describes.

My recommendation

I keep a small default stack (database and API) and put the heavy pipeline workers behind a profile, so day-to-day work does not pay for ETL. Every service gets a real healthcheck, downstream services wait on health rather than on container start, ports are bound to 127.0.0.1 and written down, and each service has a CPU and memory ceiling.

Worked example

The example below starts a Postgres database and an API by default. The worker only starts when you ask for the etl profile, and it will not start until the database reports healthy.

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: local-only-password
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:5433:5432"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M

  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
    environment:
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/postgres
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "1.0"
          memory: 512M

  etl-worker:
    build: ./worker
    profiles: ["etl"]
    environment:
      DB_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/postgres
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          cpus: "0.5"
          memory: 256M

Start the base stack and wait until everything is healthy, then add the pipeline when you need it:

docker compose up -d --wait
docker compose --profile etl up -d
docker compose ps
docker stats --no-stream

The last command is the quick check that the limits are actually applied. If a container sits at its memory ceiling, that is information, not a bug in the cap.

Checklist

  1. Put a real readiness check on every service that others depend on.
  2. Use condition: service_healthy instead of sleeps or start-order assumptions.
  3. Bind ports explicitly, to 127.0.0.1, and keep them in a small documented range.
  4. Set CPU and memory limits on every service, and make workers back off or fail with a clear message when they hit them.
  5. Mark throwaway volumes clearly and prune them on a schedule.

Where this doesn't apply

This is a local-development pattern. Profiles are a convenience that can drift from how the real system is orchestrated, so do not treat a passing local stack as proof that production wiring is right.

One honest limitation

Healthchecks add startup time, and a heavy check makes it worse. Keep them to a cheap probe, and remember that a limit set too low turns a slow job into an out-of-memory kill.

Sources

  • Docker Docs: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose
  • Docker Docs: Using profiles with Compose
  • Docker Docs: Compose deploy specification (resources)

atom:entry.atom:title: Using OCI Instance Principals without leaking credentials
atom:entry.atom:summary: How I let workloads call OCI APIs with no API keys on disk, and keep the blast radius small.
atom:entry.atom:content:
Problem

Every OCI SDK sample starts the same way: drop an API key and a config file on the host. That is fine on a laptop. On a fleet of compute instances it becomes a quiet liability, because those keys never expire on their own, they get copied into images, and nobody remembers which ones are still in use.

Instance principals remove that whole class of problem. The instance proves who it is with a certificate that OCI issues and rotates for it, and IAM decides what it may do through a dynamic group and a policy. There is nothing to ship, nothing to rotate by hand, and nothing to leak from a config file.

Options and trade-offs

  • API keys in a config file: the simplest option, but it leaves a long-lived secret on disk and puts rotation on you.
  • Session or delegation tokens: shorter lived, but you still have to mint, distribute and refresh them from somewhere.
  • Instance principals with a dynamic group: no client-side secret at all. The cost is that you have to think carefully about which instances land in the group.

My recommendation

For code running on OCI compute, I make instance principals the default and write the dynamic group rule before anything else. The rule should name a compartment and a tag, and the policy should name a compartment, a resource family and, where it is practical, a single bucket. Tenancy-wide verbs are the exception and need a reason.

Worked example

The Java below runs only on an instance that belongs to the dynamic group. It reads from one bucket and has no credentials in code, environment variables or files. The namespace and bucket name come from configuration.

import com.oracle.bmc.auth.InstancePrincipalsAuthenticationDetailsProvider;
import com.oracle.bmc.objectstorage.ObjectStorageClient;
import com.oracle.bmc.objectstorage.requests.ListObjectsRequest;
 
public class ListConfigObjects {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var provider = InstancePrincipalsAuthenticationDetailsProvider.builder().build();
        try (var os = ObjectStorageClient.builder().build(provider)) {
            var req = ListObjectsRequest.builder()
                    .namespaceName(System.getenv("OCI_NAMESPACE"))
                    .bucketName(System.getenv("CONFIG_BUCKET"))
                    .build();
            os.listObjects(req).getListObjects().getObjects()
              .forEach(o -> System.out.println(o.getName()));
        }
    }
}

The matching rule and policy for the dynamic group. The tag makes membership an explicit decision rather than a side effect of where an instance was created.

ALL {instance.compartment.id = '<apps_compartment_ocid>',
     tag.department.runtime.value = 'payments'}
 
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to read objects in compartment apps
  where target.bucket.name = 'app-config'
Allow dynamic-group app-runtimes to use log-content in compartment apps

If your dynamic group lives in a non-default identity domain, prefix the group name with the domain, for example dynamic-group MyDomain/app-runtimes.

Checklist

  1. Write the dynamic group rule with both a compartment and a tag.
  2. Grant the narrowest verb and resource family, and add a bucket or resource condition where you can.
  3. Remove every API key and config file from the host once the SDK uses the instance principal provider.
  4. Review the audit log and confirm the principal on each call is the instance you expected.
  5. Control who can apply the tag, because tagging an instance is what adds it to the group.
  6. Write down the rollback: edit the rule, then adjust the policy.

Where this doesn't apply

Serverless functions and other managed resources have their own identity, so use resource principals there. Anything running outside OCI has no instance principal at all and needs a different authentication path.

One honest limitation

Anyone who can get a shell on the instance inherits its permissions. Instance principals take away the secret, not the access, so SSH access and the policy have to be designed together.

Sources

  • OCI Documentation: Calling Services from an Instance
  • OCI Documentation: Managing Dynamic Groups
  • OCI Documentation: OCI SDK for Java, Instance Principals authentication
